考試官教諭顧　批〔體認直切。〕
大賢推尊三聖，而獨有所宗，可以見自任之重
translation_en:
…human relationships and make them a basis for conduct [?]? Thus, in the establishment of royal institutions, nothing is more important than the three weighty matters, and the inclinations of all human hearts converge upon a single unity. This is indeed the enduring achievement of the Zhou. Could anyone living in its age possibly turn against it? Moreover, Zisi’s words here carry forward the intention of honoring the Zhou. The Master was born in the closing age of the Zhou. His Way was great and his virtue vast, sufficient to qualify him to establish institutions, yet he did not occupy the requisite position. Hence he said: “I have studied the rites of Zhou; they are now in use, and I follow Zhou.” In this he went to the utmost in establishing safeguards for ten thousand generations. Zisi was one who learned from the Master. He first set forth the warning against living in the present while reverting to antiquity, then clarified it through the comprehensive unity of Zhou institutions. He thereby showed not only that those in subordinate positions must not turn against them: we can also envision the splendor of Zhou institutions in their consummate goodness and perfection. Thus, on another occasion, the Master said: “How splendid its culture!” This is what those words expressed. If students consider these statements together, they will have understood more than half of both the duty of subordinates not to turn against established authority and the sage’s intention in following Zhou.

“They were all sages of antiquity. I have not yet been able to put their ways into practice, but my wish is to learn from Confucius.”
Yang Lianfang
Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor, comments: 〔The wording is judicious, the principles clear, and the meaning fully expressed. Only this essay achieves this.〕
Examiner Yuan, Instructor, comments: 〔The discussion of the wish to learn is especially apt.〕
Examiner Gu, Instructor, comments: 〔The understanding is direct and incisive.〕
The great worthy reveres the three sages, yet takes just one as his guiding master; from this we can see the weight of the responsibility he assumes…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
矣夫孔子道之宗也大賢竝尊三聖而獨有志
於孔子其自任以斯道之重也如此此孟子折
衷之論以見夷尹不同道也意謂大哉聖人之
道自其造夫極者而言不可或謂之異自其會
夫全者而觀不可咸謂之同吾嘗仰而思之伯
夷以道自潔聖之清者也伊尹以道救民聖之
任者也孔子以道行權聖之時者也是皆成性
安行而無事彊勉為道不同同歸於聖人之域
矣亦嘗內而省之所求乎夷清何有於我也所
===
求乎尹任何有於我也所求乎孔子時何有於
我也是蓋遠慕近守而躬行未逮為聖不同同
歟於克卣之難矣夫行固未能而志則不可不
辨也乃若所願舍孔子何適乎惟孔子道深於
化或仕或止旁行而不流凡夷尹之行夫固兼
體而無累也聖集其成或久或速變易而不居
凡清任之道夫固神化而無方也我則幸餘澤
之未泯而私淑之仕其所當仕焉止其所當止
焉道之所在固其神之相為潛孚焉者矣外此
punctuated: 矣。夫孔子，道之宗也。大賢竝尊三聖，而獨有志於孔子，其自任以斯道之重也如此。此孟子折衷之論，以見夷尹不同道也。意謂：大哉，聖人之道！自其造夫極者而言，不可或謂之異；自其會夫全者而觀，不可咸謂之同。吾嘗仰而思之：伯夷以道自潔，聖之清者也；伊尹以道救民，聖之任者也；孔子以道行權，聖之時者也。是皆成性安行，而無事彊勉；為道不同，同歸於聖人之域矣。亦嘗內而省之：所求乎夷清，何有於我也？所求乎尹任，何有於我也？所求乎孔子時，何有於我也？是蓋遠慕近守，而躬行未逮；為聖不同，同歟於克卣之難矣。夫行固未能，而志則不可不辨也。乃若所願，舍孔子何適乎？惟孔子道深於化，或仕或止，旁行而不流，凡夷尹之行，夫固兼體而無累也。聖集其成，或久或速，變易而不居，凡清任之道，夫固神化而無方也。我則幸餘澤之未泯，而私淑之。仕其所當仕焉，止其所當止焉，道之所在，固其神之相為潛孚焉者矣。外此
translation_en:
…indeed. Confucius is the supreme exemplar of the Way. The great worthy revered all three sages alike, yet set his aspirations upon Confucius alone: such was the weight of responsibility for this Way that he took upon himself. This is Mencius’s considered judgment, showing that Bo Yi and Yi Yin followed different paths. Its meaning is as follows: How great is the Way of the sages! Speaking of their attainment of the ultimate, one cannot say that any differed; considering their comprehensive realization of the whole, one cannot say that all were alike.

I have looked up to them and reflected: Bo Yi kept himself pure through the Way; he was the pure one among the sages. Yi Yin saved the people through the Way; he was the responsible one among the sages. Confucius exercised discretionary judgment through the Way; he was the timely one among the sages. All fully realized their nature and acted with ease, without needing forced effort. Though their practice of the Way differed, they all reached the realm of sagehood. I have also examined myself inwardly: Of the purity sought in Bo Yi, what do I possess? Of the responsibility sought in Yi Yin, what do I possess? Of the timeliness sought in Confucius, what do I possess? I admire them from afar and hold fast to what lies close at hand, yet my own conduct has not caught up. Their ways of being sages differed, but the difficulty of mastering oneself is shared [?].

Although I have not yet attained their conduct, I must distinguish clearly where my aspirations lie. As for what I desire, where could I turn if I forsook Confucius? Confucius alone followed the Way to the depths of transformation: sometimes entering office, sometimes withdrawing, ranging widely without drifting astray. He fully embodied the conduct of both Bo Yi and Yi Yin without being encumbered by either. His sagehood brought their achievements together into a complete whole: sometimes remaining long, sometimes departing swiftly, changing without being fixed in one position. The ways of purity and responsibility alike were wondrously transformed in him, unrestricted by any fixed method.

I count myself fortunate that his lingering influence has not vanished, and I cultivate myself through it, though unable to learn from him directly. I enter office when it is fitting to enter office and withdraw when it is fitting to withdraw. Wherever the Way lies, our spirits surely accord with one another unseen. Beyond this…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
而夷而尹豈吾之所學哉仰師資之有托而思
齊之久其所當久焉速其所當速焉時之所在
固其志之相爲默契焉者矣外此而清而任豈
吾之所學哉是夷也尹也非真不可學也但一
於清者或遺憂世之志偏於任者有累樂天之
誠清任固非我所能實非我所安也此吾之所
以與夷尹不同道也而丑爲我願之乎抑伯夷
百世之師也伊尹先覺之聖也孟子既以聖稱
矣而玆獨宗孔子然則聖人亦有不足法乎葢
===
孔子者元氣之流行於四時也夷尹者四時之
各居其一也故孔子之時非出乎清任之外而
夷尹之清任卽寓夫時之中但夷尹執之而孔
子化之也孟子之願學孔子正所以善學二子
也孰謂孟子果不法夷尹哉
易
先天而天弗違後天而奉天時
張鵬翰
同考試官教諭林　批〔發明先天後天無券鑿痕濬 心〕
punctuated:
而夷而尹，豈吾之所學哉？仰師資之有托而思齊之，久其所當久焉，速其所當速焉。時之所在，固其志之相爲默契焉者矣。外此而清而任，豈吾之所學哉？是夷也、尹也，非真不可學也。但一於清者，或遺憂世之志；偏於任者，有累樂天之誠。清任固非我所能，實非我所安也。此吾之所以與夷尹不同道也，而丑爲我願之乎？抑伯夷，百世之師也；伊尹，先覺之聖也。孟子既以聖稱矣，而玆獨宗孔子，然則聖人亦有不足法乎？葢孔子者，元氣之流行於四時也；夷尹者，四時之各居其一也。故孔子之時，非出乎清任之外，而夷尹之清任，卽寓夫時之中。但夷尹執之，而孔子化之也。孟子之願學孔子，正所以善學二子也。孰謂孟子果不法夷尹哉？

易
先天而天弗違，後天而奉天時。
張鵬翰
同考試官教諭林　批〔發明先天後天無券鑿痕濬 心〕
translation_en:
…to follow Bo Yi or Yi Yin beyond this—could that be what I seek to learn? Looking up to a teacher on whom I can rely, I aspire to equal him: remaining when it is fitting to remain, and departing promptly when it is fitting to depart. Wherever the circumstances of the time require, our intentions surely accord in silent understanding. Beyond this, could purity or taking responsibility alone be what I seek to learn? It is not that Bo Yi and Yi Yin truly cannot be emulated. Yet exclusive devotion to purity may neglect the resolve to care for the world; partiality toward taking responsibility may compromise the sincerity of delighting in Heaven. Such purity and responsibility are indeed beyond my ability, and truly are not what puts my heart at ease. This is why I do not follow the same path as Bo Yi and Yi Yin. Yet you, Chou, would wish this for me?

But Bo Yi was a teacher for a hundred generations, and Yi Yin a sage who attained understanding before others. Since Mengzi called them sages, yet here takes Confucius alone as his master, does this mean that even sages are in some respect inadequate as models? Confucius is like the primal vital force circulating through the four seasons; Bo Yi and Yi Yin are each like just one of those seasons. Thus Confucius’s timeliness does not lie outside purity and responsibility, while the purity and responsibility of Bo Yi and Yi Yin are themselves contained within timeliness. It is simply that Bo Yi and Yi Yin held fast to these principles, whereas Confucius transformed them. Mengzi’s wish to learn from Confucius was precisely how he could best learn from those two masters. Who could say that Mengzi truly did not take Bo Yi and Yi Yin as models?

Book of Changes
“When he precedes Heaven, Heaven does not oppose him; when he follows Heaven, he accords with Heaven’s seasons.”

Zhang Penghan

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, a School Instructor: 〔Elucidates preceding Heaven and following Heaven without traces of forced chiseling [?]; profound in mind [?] …〕

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
蕐學亦有得者
考試官敎諭袁　批〔詞意精緻〕
考試官敎諭顧　批〔明煢〕
大人之於天隨所爲而皆合也蓋天者理而已
矣大人先天後天而一之以理此所以無所爲
而不合也與文言發乾九五利見之義也至此
意謂理一而已矣天得之而爲天大人得之而
爲大人者也九五之所以爲大人而利見者豈
特天地日月四時鬼神之合而已哉今夫理涵
===
於太始而前無所徵大人則以意而先之竭心
思以代天之工創制作以前民之用夫是之謂
先天也先天而爲之若難必其弗違矣然天者
道之大原也大人以道爲體而心與之契故其
所已爲者皆天心之所欲爲者也況幾足以開
先而命自我出建之而不悖明哲足以作則而
道自我立推之而皆準裁成其道而天地於我
乎範圍也輔相其宜而萬物於我乎曲成也存
之也而卽神過之也而卽化人固爲之天固順
punctuated:
蕐學亦有得者。
考試官敎諭袁，批〔詞意精緻〕。
考試官敎諭顧，批〔明煢〕。
大人之於天，隨所爲而皆合也。蓋天者，理而已矣。大人先天後天，而一之以理，此所以無所爲而不合也與！《文言》發乾九五利見之義也，至此，意謂理一而已矣，天得之而爲天，大人得之而爲大人者也。九五之所以爲大人而利見者，豈特天地日月四時鬼神之合而已哉？今夫理涵於太始，而前無所徵，大人則以意而先之，竭心思以代天之工，創制作以前民之用，夫是之謂先天也。先天而爲之，若難必其弗違矣。然天者，道之大原也。大人以道爲體，而心與之契，故其所已爲者，皆天心之所欲爲者也。況幾足以開先，而命自我出，建之而不悖；明哲足以作則，而道自我立，推之而皆準。裁成其道，而天地於我乎範圍也；輔相其宜，而萬物於我乎曲成也。存之也而卽神，過之也而卽化。人固爲之，天固順
translation_en:
… also possesses attainment in learning [?].
Examiner Yuan, Instructor, comments: 〔The language and ideas are finely wrought.〕
Examiner Gu, Instructor, comments: 〔Clear [?].〕
In his relation to Heaven, the great man accords with it in whatever he does. For Heaven is nothing other than principle. Whether the great man precedes Heaven or follows Heaven, he unifies both through principle. Is this not why nothing he does fails to accord with Heaven? The Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan) elucidates the meaning of “it is beneficial to see” in the fifth, yang line of Qian. At this point, its meaning is that principle is one: Heaven obtains it and thereby becomes Heaven; the great man obtains it and thereby becomes a great man. Can the reason that the fifth, yang line represents the great man, whom it is beneficial to see, be merely his accord with Heaven and Earth, the sun and moon, the four seasons, and ghosts and spirits?
Now, when principle lies concealed in the primordial beginning and there is no prior evidence by which to discern it, the great man anticipates it through his intent. He exhausts his mental powers to perform Heaven’s work on its behalf, and originates institutions and undertakings to anticipate the people’s needs. This is what is meant by preceding Heaven. When he acts before Heaven, it might seem difficult to be certain that Heaven will not run counter to him. Yet Heaven is the great source of the Way. The great man takes the Way as his substance, and his mind accords with it; thus, all that he has already done is what Heaven’s mind wishes to do.
Moreover, his discernment of incipient developments suffices to take the lead: commands issue from him, and what he establishes does not conflict with principle. His wisdom suffices to create standards: the Way is established through him, and wherever it is extended it provides a norm. He regulates and completes their Way, and Heaven and Earth are thereby brought within his compass. He assists what is fitting for them, and the myriad things are thereby brought to fulfillment in all their particulars. Where he abides, there is spiritual efficacy; where he passes, there is transformation. Man indeed acts, and Heaven indeed follows …

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
之是謂洩天之秘而人之未始不爲天矣天寧
違於大人乎故謂大人與天同體亦可也至若
道著於有象而後有可法大人則奉天而行之
盡人以終天地之功尚象以成天下之利夫是
之謂後天也後天而奉之自有以應乎時矣蓋
時者理之當然也大人與理爲徒而身與之俱
故其所自爲者皆天則之所可見者也察天理
以左右而欽崇時憲因其已然之迹順帝則以
周旋而識變達化法其自然之運以行典禮則
===
天叙天秩因物而付物也以順休命則天命天
討與時而偕行也窮神而善繼其志知化而善
述其事天固始之人固承之是謂成天之能而
天之未始不爲人矣大人寧違於天乎故謂大
人與天同用亦可也是則天不違乎大人大人
一天也大人奉若乎天時天一大人也天與大
人相爲後先矣而夫人之利見也烏容已哉抑
天人一理也聖人之與途人一性也大人之所
以與天合一者豈有加於性分之外哉盡其性
punctuated:
之，是謂洩天之秘，而人之未始不爲天矣。天寧違於大人乎？故謂大人與天同體，亦可也。
至若道著於有象而後有可法，大人則奉天而行之，盡人以終天地之功，尚象以成天下之利，夫是之謂後天也。後天而奉之，自有以應乎時矣。蓋時者，理之當然也。大人與理爲徒，而身與之俱，故其所自爲者，皆天則之所可見者也。察天理以左右，而欽崇時憲，因其已然之迹；順帝則以周旋，而識變達化，法其自然之運。以行典禮，則天叙天秩，因物而付物也；以順休命，則天命天討，與時而偕行也。窮神而善繼其志，知化而善述其事。天固始之，人固承之，是謂成天之能，而天之未始不爲人矣。大人寧違於天乎？故謂大人與天同用，亦可也。
是則天不違乎大人，大人一天也；大人奉若乎天時，天一大人也。天與大人相爲後先矣，而夫人之利見也，烏容已哉？抑天人一理也，聖人之與途人一性也。大人之所以與天合一者，豈有加於性分之外哉？盡其性
translation_en:
…it. This is called revealing Heaven’s secrets: human action has never been other than Heaven’s action. How could Heaven go against the great man? Thus one may also say that the great man shares one substance with Heaven.
When the Way becomes manifest in perceptible forms, providing models to follow, the great man reverently follows Heaven and puts them into practice. He exhausts human capacities to complete the work of Heaven and Earth, and esteems their images to bring benefits to all under Heaven. This is what is meant by acting after Heaven. By acting after Heaven and reverently following it, he naturally has the means to respond to the times. For what the times require is what principle dictates. The great man takes principle as his companion and embodies it in his conduct; thus all that he does makes Heaven’s standards visible. He examines Heaven’s principle to guide and assist its workings, reverently honoring the ordinances of the seasons and following the traces of what has already come to pass. He follows the Supreme Ruler’s standards in all his actions, discerning change and comprehending transformation, taking their spontaneous workings as his model. In carrying out established rites, he implements Heaven’s ordering of relationships and ranking of distinctions, assigning each thing its due according to its nature. In obeying Heaven’s beneficent mandate, he confers Heaven’s appointments and executes Heaven’s punishments, acting in step with the times. He fathoms the numinous and thus skillfully carries forward Heaven’s intent; he understands transformation and thus skillfully carries on Heaven’s work. Heaven initiates it, and the human being takes it up. This is called bringing Heaven’s capacity to completion: Heaven’s action has never been other than human action. How could the great man go against Heaven? Thus one may also say that the great man shares one function with Heaven.
Hence, when Heaven does not go against the great man, the great man is a Heaven; when the great man reverently accords with Heaven’s seasons, Heaven is a great man. Heaven and the great man take turns preceding and following each other. How, then, could people ever cease to find it beneficial to behold him? Yet Heaven and humanity share one principle, and the sage and the ordinary passerby share one nature. In becoming one with Heaven, does the great man add anything beyond what is allotted to his nature? He fully realizes his nature…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
而不以己私與焉耳自私則狹狹則有外有外
之心不足以合天始以大人爲神異絕德不可
企及而自外於天矣君子希聖以希天故不求
天之迹而求忘己之私其道成於無我而其究
終於達天是亦大人而已矣故曰大人者不失
其赤子之心者也
夫易廣矣大矣以言乎遠則不禦以言乎
邇則静而正以言乎天地之間則備矣
楊緯
同考試官教諭林　批〔廣大即曽是遠邇天地之間作者〕
===
大傳論易道之廣大必指其所在以見之也蓋
易者陰陽之理也舉遠近天地而理無不在易
之廣大不於是而見乎夫子賛易之意也謂夫
天下之理莫外於陰陽陰陽之義莫辯於易易
之爲道可以易言耶自其外而觀之冒天下
考試官教諭顧　批〔簡切〕
考試官教諭袁　批〔明建庫淨〕
〔頗知之發明不浮則重乏作理明而辭不泛遂於易者〕
punctuated:
而不以己私與焉耳。自私則狹，狹則有外；有外之心，不足以合天，始以大人爲神異絕德，不可企及，而自外於天矣。君子希聖以希天，故不求天之迹，而求忘己之私。其道成於無我，而其究終於達天，是亦大人而已矣。故曰：「大人者，不失其赤子之心者也。」
夫易廣矣，大矣！以言乎遠，則不禦；以言乎邇，則静而正；以言乎天地之間，則備矣。
楊緯
同考試官教諭林，批〔廣大即曽是遠邇天地之間作者〕
大傳論易道之廣大，必指其所在以見之也。蓋易者，陰陽之理也。舉遠近天地，而理無不在，易之廣大不於是而見乎？夫子賛易之意也，謂夫天下之理，莫外於陰陽；陰陽之義，莫辯於易。易之爲道，可以易言耶？自其外而觀之，冒天下
考試官教諭顧，批〔簡切〕
考試官教諭袁，批〔明建庫淨〕
〔頗知之發明不浮則重乏作理明而辭不泛遂於易者〕
translation_en:
…and merely refrains from allowing his own selfish interests to intrude. Selfishness leads to narrowness, and narrowness leads to excluding what lies outside oneself. A mind that excludes cannot unite with Heaven. One then begins to regard the great man as a wondrous being of peerless virtue, impossible to emulate or equal, and thereby excludes oneself from Heaven. The gentleman aspires to sagehood in order to aspire to Heaven. Thus he does not seek Heaven’s outward traces, but seeks to forget his own selfish interests. His Way is perfected in selflessness, and its ultimate culmination is in comprehending Heaven. This, too, is simply to be a great man. Hence the saying: “The great man is one who does not lose the heart of a newborn child.”
“The Changes is broad indeed, and great indeed! Speaking of what is distant, it encounters no bounds; speaking of what is near, it is still and correct; speaking of what lies between Heaven and Earth, it is complete.”
Yang Wei.
Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: 〔“Broad and great” refers precisely to [?] the distant, the near, and what lies between Heaven and Earth; the author … [?]〕
When the Great Commentary discusses the breadth and greatness of the Way of the Changes, it necessarily points to where that Way is found in order to make it manifest. For the Changes is the principle of yin and yang. Throughout the distant and the near, Heaven and Earth, there is nowhere this principle is absent. Is not the breadth and greatness of the Changes manifest in this? This is the Master’s intention in elucidating the Changes: no principle under Heaven lies outside yin and yang, and nowhere is the meaning of yin and yang more clearly distinguished than in the Changes. Can the Way of the Changes be spoken of lightly? Viewed from without, it encompasses all under Heaven …
Examiner Gu, Instructor, comments: 〔Concise and pertinent.〕
Examiner Yuan, Instructor, comments: 〔Clear … [?]〕
〔Shows considerable understanding in its elucidation; not superficial … [?] The principle is clear and the language does not stray into generalities … the Changes [?].〕

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
之道而無所不包自其內而觀之立天下之有
而無所不具其諸廣矣大矣乎何以見之彼天
下之理語遠則易限若或禦之矣易則遠而不
禦通於有形之外推之而莫知所止運乎不息
之幾究之而莫知所終蓋有以見乎是理之無
窮盡矣其孰得而禦之天下之理語近則易窒
若或遺之矣易則以靜而正天然自有之妙而
纖微之必察一理流行之實而須臾之無間蓋
有以見乎是理之無滲漏矣有不靜而正乎極
===
而言之天高地下萬物散殊言乎其間則盡乎
其有矣然天地是理之法象也萬物是理之發
育也成位之設莫非變化之所行竝育之間莫
非擬議之所及蓋又有以見乎是理之全體而
無餘矣天地之間有未備耶夫言廣大而遠近
天地盡之矣言遠近天地而易理盡之矣此易
之所以廣大而無以復加矣乎大哉易也斯其
至矣抑廣大之理具於易然不自易始也本於
天地而通於人心故易知者自大簡能者自廣
punctuated: 之道而無所不包；自其內而觀之，立天下之有而無所不具。其諸廣矣大矣乎！何以見之？彼天下之理，語遠則易限，若或禦之矣；易則遠而不禦，通於有形之外，推之而莫知所止；運乎不息之幾，究之而莫知所終。蓋有以見乎是理之無窮盡矣，其孰得而禦之？天下之理，語近則易窒，若或遺之矣；易則以靜而正，天然自有之妙，而纖微之必察；一理流行之實，而須臾之無間。蓋有以見乎是理之無滲漏矣，有不靜而正乎？極而言之，天高地下，萬物散殊，言乎其間，則盡乎其有矣。然天地，是理之法象也；萬物，是理之發育也。成位之設，莫非變化之所行；竝育之間，莫非擬議之所及。蓋又有以見乎是理之全體而無餘矣，天地之間有未備耶？夫言廣大，而遠近天地盡之矣；言遠近天地，而易理盡之矣。此易之所以廣大而無以復加矣乎！大哉易也，斯其至矣！抑廣大之理具於易，然不自易始也，本於天地而通於人心。故易知者自大，簡能者自廣。
translation_en:
…the ways of all under Heaven, encompassing everything; viewed from within, it establishes all that exists under Heaven, lacking nothing. How broad and great it must be! How can this be seen? As for the principles of all under Heaven, when one speaks of what is distant, one readily encounters limits, as though something were blocking them. The Changes, however, reaches far without obstruction. It extends beyond what has form: pursue it, and no one knows where it stops. It operates through the ceaseless incipience of change: investigate it, and no one knows where it ends. Here we can see that this principle is inexhaustible. Who could obstruct it? As for the principles of all under Heaven, when one speaks of what is near, one readily becomes hemmed in, as though something had been omitted. The Changes, however, is still and correct. In its inherently natural subtlety, even the minutest detail is invariably discerned; in the actual circulation of the single principle, there is not a moment’s interruption. Here we can see that this principle allows nothing to slip through. Could it fail to be still and correct?

To speak of the utmost extent: Heaven is high, Earth is low, and the myriad things are dispersed and differentiated. To speak of what lies between them is to encompass all that exists. Yet Heaven and Earth are the exemplary manifestations of this principle, and the myriad things are its unfolding and nourishment. The ordering of established positions is everywhere the operation of transformation; among things nurtured together, nothing lies beyond the reach of comparison and deliberation. Here, moreover, we can see the entirety of this principle, with nothing left over. Is anything between Heaven and Earth unaccounted for? When we speak of breadth and greatness, the distant and the near, Heaven and Earth, exhaust their scope. When we speak of the distant and the near, Heaven and Earth, the principle of the Changes exhausts their scope. Is this not why the Changes is so broad and great that nothing more can be added? Great indeed is the Changes! Here it reaches the utmost!

Yet although the principle of breadth and greatness is fully present in the Changes, it did not originate with the Changes. It is rooted in Heaven and Earth and pervades the human heart-mind. Thus, that which knows through ease is inherently great, and that which accomplishes through simplicity is inherently broad…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
大者吾心之易而廣者吾心之簡也聖人作易
亦因所本有而模寫之是以建之不悖而用之
盡神者也故曰易簡而天下之理得矣學易者
不求之易而求之吾心則廣大可致而至理在
我易書者特吾心之糟粕耳此固畫前有易之
意而善學者自得之
書
乃聖乃神乃武乃文
楊聯芳
同考試官教諭周 批 渾融精密佳作也
考試官教諭袁 批 善形容堯德
考試官教諭顧 批 精確得旨
===
大臣之贊帝堯歷名其爲德之盛焉甚矣大哉
堯之爲德充周而不可窮者也則其妙變化而
極名言之盛也有以哉昔伯益因帝舜以克艱
歸美於堯乃贊堯之德而寓致望於舜之意也
謂夫后惟克艱而後能以成天下之大治堯允
克艱而實有以備天下之盛美帝固念之請爲
punctuated:
大者，吾心之易，而廣者，吾心之簡也。聖人作易，亦因所本有而模寫之，是以建之不悖而用之盡神者也。故曰：「易簡而天下之理得矣。」學易者，不求之易而求之吾心，則廣大可致而至理在我，易書者特吾心之糟粕耳。此固畫前有易之意，而善學者自得之。

書
「乃聖乃神乃武乃文」
楊聯芳
同考試官教諭周批：「渾融精密，佳作也。」
考試官教諭袁批：「善形容堯德。」
考試官教諭顧批：「精確得旨。」

大臣之贊帝堯，歷名其爲德之盛焉。甚矣，大哉，堯之爲德！充周而不可窮者也，則其妙變化而極名言之盛也，有以哉！昔伯益因帝舜以克艱歸美於堯，乃贊堯之德，而寓致望於舜之意也。謂夫后惟克艱，而後能以成天下之大治；堯允克艱，而實有以備天下之盛美。帝固念之，請爲
translation_en:
…Greatness is the ease within my own mind, and breadth is the simplicity within my own mind. When the sage composed the Changes, he likewise depicted what was inherently present. Thus what he established was without contradiction, and its application fully realized spiritual efficacy. Hence it is said: “Through ease and simplicity, the principles of all under Heaven are apprehended.” If students of the Changes seek this within their own minds rather than in the Changes, breadth and greatness can be attained, and the ultimate principle resides within themselves. The book of Changes is merely the dregs of one's own mind. This is precisely the meaning of the saying that the Changes existed before the hexagram lines were drawn; those who learn well apprehend it for themselves.

Book of Documents
“He was sagely, spiritually perceptive, martial, and cultured.”
Yang Lianfang
Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor, comments: “Harmoniously integrated, refined, and meticulous: an excellent composition.”
Examiner Yuan, Instructor, comments: “It portrays Yao's virtue well.”
Examiner Gu, Instructor, comments: “Precise and accurate; it grasps the purport.”

In praising Emperor Yao, the great minister enumerated the qualities of his abundant virtue. How surpassingly great was Yao's virtue! It pervaded everything and could not be exhausted. There was good reason, then, that its wondrous transformations called forth the fullest expressions of praise. Formerly, when Emperor Shun credited Yao with the ability to confront the difficulties of rulership, Bo Yi praised Yao's virtue, thereby also conveying his hopes for Shun. His meaning was that only by confronting these difficulties could a ruler bring about great order throughout the realm. Yao truly could confront them, and thus possessed in full all the finest qualities under Heaven. “Your Majesty surely bears this in mind. Allow me, for…”

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
帝陳之蓋帝堯之德惟其至廣而妙運是故變
化而無方有所謂聖者焉知周萬物無思而無
不通明炳幾先不習而無不利其德性則安安
也其德行則允克也是蓋大而化之何有於強
何有於爲乃其聖矣然且妙至德於淵微而莫
得以窺其際泯機緘於默運而莫知其所以然
不疾而自速焉不行而自至焉何其神也夫聖
矣而又神焉則聖而不可知也其視大化流行
而於穆不已者不其同神已乎有所謂武者焉
===
發強剛毅神武涵不殺之威靜重端凝德威儼
惟畏之象不怒而自肅也不戒而自孚也是蓋
握乾之斷以震萬幾以正萬民乃其武矣然又
發文思之英華而丕顯于一身麗開物之經緯
而光被乎四表煥乎其有文章焉天地將爲昭
焉何其文也夫武矣而又文焉蓋聖作而物覩
也其視春生秋殺而竝行不悖者不其合德已
乎是則聖神文武一廣運也廣運一天也天以
廣運而行化工堯以廣運而神變化故曰惟天
punctuated: 帝陳之。蓋帝堯之德，惟其至廣而妙運，是故變化而無方，有所謂聖者焉。知周萬物，無思而無不通；明炳幾先，不習而無不利。其德性則安安也，其德行則允克也。是蓋大而化之，何有於強？何有於爲？乃其聖矣。然且妙至德於淵微，而莫得以窺其際；泯機緘於默運，而莫知其所以然。不疾而自速焉，不行而自至焉，何其神也！夫聖矣而又神焉，則聖而不可知也。其視大化流行而於穆不已者，不其同神已乎？有所謂武者焉：發強剛毅，神武涵不殺之威；靜重端凝，德威儼惟畏之象。不怒而自肅也，不戒而自孚也。是蓋握乾之斷，以震萬幾，以正萬民，乃其武矣。然又發文思之英華，而丕顯于一身；麗開物之經緯，而光被乎四表。煥乎其有文章焉，天地將爲昭焉，何其文也！夫武矣而又文焉，蓋聖作而物覩也。其視春生秋殺而竝行不悖者，不其合德已乎？是則聖神文武，一廣運也；廣運，一天也。天以廣運而行化工，堯以廣運而神變化。故曰：「惟天
translation_en:
…set it forth for Your Majesty. Emperor Yao’s virtue was supremely expansive and wondrous in its operation; thus its transformations were without fixed bounds. Herein lies what is called sageliness. His understanding encompassed all things: without deliberation, there was nothing he did not comprehend. His discernment illuminated events before their first stirrings: without practice, there was nothing in which he was not adept. In his virtuous nature he was effortlessly at ease; in his virtuous conduct he was truly capable. This was greatness transformed into sageliness. What need was there for exertion? What need for deliberate action? Such was his sageliness. Moreover, he brought supreme virtue to wondrous expression in its profound subtleties, so that none could glimpse its limits; he concealed the workings of its inner mechanism in silent operation, so that none could know how it came to be so. Without haste, it was swift of itself; without movement, it arrived of itself. How spiritual it was! To be sagely and also spiritual is to be sagely beyond comprehension. Compared with the ceaseless flow of the great cosmic transformation, profound and unending, did he not share its spiritual efficacy?

There was also what is called martial might. Energetic, strong, firm, and resolute, his spiritual martial power contained an awe-inspiring force that did not kill. Still, grave, upright, and composed, his virtuous authority presented a solemn aspect that commanded reverence. Without anger, he naturally inspired solemn respect; without admonition, he naturally inspired trust. He wielded the decisiveness of Qian, the Creative, to stir the myriad affairs of government and set the myriad people aright. Such was his martial might. Yet he also brought forth the finest flowering of cultivated thought, making it greatly manifest in his own person; he displayed the ordered patterns through which all things are brought to fulfillment, spreading his radiance to the four outer bounds. How resplendent were his patterned accomplishments! Heaven and earth themselves would be illumined by them. How cultivated he was! To possess martial might and also cultural refinement is indeed for the sage to arise and all things to come into view. Compared with spring’s generation and autumn’s destruction, which proceed together without conflict, did he not unite with them in virtue?

Thus sageliness, spiritual efficacy, cultural refinement, and martial might were all one expansive operation; and this expansive operation was one with Heaven. Through its expansive operation, Heaven performs the work of transformation; through his expansive operation, Yao made his transformations spiritually wondrous. Hence it is said: “Only Heaven…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
爲大惟堯則之抑謂堯之德如此其盛即所謂
峻德也峻德難名故曰蕩蕩乎民無能名焉而
以聖神文武名之者就其難名者擬之而不可
以執一名耳故其德之所及至於被四表而格
上下亦如此其極也舜之玄德亦峻德也紹堯
致治乃曰重華要其德之所以盛亦惟執中焉
爾中則與天合一而其本則原于心此堯舜心
德之授受實萬世道統之宗
六卿分職各率其屬以倡九牧阜成兆民
===
蔡賓
同考試官教諭周 批〔氣格春容辭理蔚甚可以爲文矣〕
考試官教諭袁 批〔純精可則〕
考試官教諭顧 批〔典雅〕
賢王訓六卿立圖治之體以安民也夫六卿中
外之紀而民之休戚繫焉體統立而治道彰矣
民其有不安者乎昔成王撫承平之運而不忘
乎保治之圖鑒前代之規而因制夫訓官之體
punctuated:
爲大，惟堯則之。抑謂堯之德如此其盛，即所謂峻德也。峻德難名，故曰：「蕩蕩乎，民無能名焉。」而以聖神文武名之者，就其難名者擬之，而不可以執一名耳。故其德之所及，至於被四表而格上下，亦如此其極也。舜之玄德，亦峻德也。紹堯致治，乃曰重華。要其德之所以盛，亦惟執中焉爾。中則與天合一，而其本則原于心。此堯舜心德之授受，實萬世道統之宗。

六卿分職，各率其屬，以倡九牧，阜成兆民。

蔡賓

同考試官教諭周批〔氣格春容，辭理蔚甚，可以爲文矣。〕
考試官教諭袁批〔純精可則。〕
考試官教諭顧批〔典雅。〕

賢王訓六卿，立圖治之體以安民也。夫六卿，中外之紀，而民之休戚繫焉。體統立而治道彰矣，民其有不安者乎？昔成王撫承平之運，而不忘乎保治之圖，鑒前代之規，而因制夫訓官之體。
translation_en:
…is great; Yao alone modeled himself upon it. Indeed, the abundance of Yao’s virtue was precisely what is called “exalted virtue.” Exalted virtue is difficult to name; thus it is said: “So vast was it that the people could find no name for it.” To describe him as sagely, spiritually perceptive, cultured, and martial is to approximate what is difficult to name, without confining it to any single designation. Thus the reach of his virtue, extending to the four outermost regions and reaching above and below, was likewise utmost. Shun’s profound virtue was also exalted virtue. His succession to Yao in bringing about good government was therefore called “renewed brilliance.” Ultimately, the abundance of his virtue lay simply in holding fast to the Mean. Through the Mean one becomes united with Heaven, and its foundation originates in the heart. This transmission and reception of the virtue of the heart between Yao and Shun is truly the source of the succession of the Way for all ages.

“The six ministers divide their duties, each leading his subordinates, to guide the nine regional governors and bring prosperity and fulfillment to the myriad people.”

Cai Bin

Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor, comments: “Its spirit and style have a springlike ease [?]; its language and reasoning are richly developed. This qualifies as accomplished composition.”
Examiner Yuan, Instructor, comments: “Pure and refined, worthy of emulation.”
Examiner Gu, Instructor, comments: “Classical and elegant.”

The worthy king instructed the six ministers, establishing the framework for pursuing good government in order to bring peace to the people. The six ministers provide the organizing structure for the capital and the regions, and the people’s well-being or suffering depends upon them. Once this framework is established and the Way of government made manifest, could any among the people remain without peace? Formerly, King Cheng presided over an age of settled peace, yet did not forget plans for preserving good government. Taking the institutions of earlier ages as his guide, he accordingly established the form of instructions for officials…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
至此若曰朝廷之政隸於六典而九州之治宗
於六官無非為生民計也惟爾六卿自冡宰而
司徒而宗伯其職則邦治邦教邦禮而有六十
屬之相承以分攝焉燦然典章之具在又自司
馬而司寇而司空其職則邦政邦禁邦土而有
六十屬之分理以相從焉昭然法制之有常是
惟率作以興事卿舉其端屬業其緒而秩秩乎
天職之是脩綱舉而目張屬效其能卿考其成
而濟濟乎天工之是亮夫政之在朝為四方之
===
極而內以達外實州牧之表六職倡之九牧則
從而宣之相維之勢無往不協庶政以之而脩
明內度先之外治則從而播之相應之機無遠
不届萬化以之而敷洽九州之民其生未易遂
也于是推之無不準而被澤潤於無外樂其樂
利其利熙熙然有以厚其生唐虞之所謂咸寧者
當不專美於前矣兆民之衆其性未易齊也于
是動之無不化而漸德教於四訖會其極歸其
極皐然有以化于中夏商之所謂用乂者將復
punctuated: 至此，若曰：朝廷之政隸於六典，而九州之治宗於六官，無非為生民計也。惟爾六卿，自冡宰而司徒而宗伯，其職則邦治、邦教、邦禮，而有六十屬之相承以分攝焉，燦然典章之具在。又自司馬而司寇而司空，其職則邦政、邦禁、邦土，而有六十屬之分理以相從焉，昭然法制之有常。是惟率作以興事，卿舉其端，屬業其緒，而秩秩乎天職之是脩；綱舉而目張，屬效其能，卿考其成，而濟濟乎天工之是亮。夫政之在朝，為四方之極，而內以達外，實州牧之表。六職倡之，九牧則從而宣之，相維之勢，無往不協，庶政以之而脩明；內度先之，外治則從而播之，相應之機，無遠不届，萬化以之而敷洽。九州之民，其生未易遂也，于是推之無不準，而被澤潤於無外，樂其樂，利其利，熙熙然有以厚其生，唐虞之所謂咸寧者，當不專美於前矣。兆民之衆，其性未易齊也，于是動之無不化，而漸德教於四訖，會其極，歸其極，皐然有以化于中，夏商之所謂用乂者，將復
translation_en:
…At this point, it was as though he said: The government of the court is governed by the six canons, and the administration of the nine regions takes the six ministries as its guiding authority. All of this is intended for the welfare of the people. You six ministers—from the Grand Steward to the Minister of Education and the Minister of Rites—are responsible respectively for the realm’s governance, instruction, and ritual. Each has sixty subordinate officers serving in succession beneath him and sharing responsibility for these duties. Thus the full array of institutions and regulations stands splendidly established. Likewise, the Minister of War, the Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Works are responsible respectively for the realm’s military affairs, prohibitions, and lands. Each has sixty subordinate officers who divide the administration among themselves and serve under him. Thus the constancy of laws and institutions is clearly manifest.

Lead them in their work to set affairs in motion: the ministers initiate undertakings, and their subordinates carry the work forward, so that the duties entrusted by Heaven are discharged in orderly fashion. When the main cord of the net is raised, its meshes spread out: the subordinates exercise their abilities, and the ministers assess their achievements, so that Heaven’s work is accomplished through their concerted efforts. Government at court provides the standard for the four quarters; extending from the center to the regions, it is indeed the model for the regional governors. When the six ministries take the lead, the governors of the nine regions follow and promulgate their measures. Their mutually sustaining relationship brings harmony everywhere, and all affairs of government are thereby put in good order. When standards at the center take precedence, administration in the regions follows and disseminates them. Their responsive interaction reaches even the most distant places, and transforming influence thereby spreads everywhere.

It is no easy matter to secure the livelihood of the people of the nine regions. Yet when these measures are extended, everyone finds a standard to follow, and the nourishing benefits reach everywhere without exception. Taking pleasure in what brings the people pleasure and advancing what benefits them, the rulers enable them to flourish happily in their livelihoods. The universal peace spoken of under Tang and Yu would then no longer be a distinction belonging exclusively to antiquity.

It is no easy matter to bring the dispositions of the countless people into accord. Yet when they are stirred to action, none fails to be transformed, and moral instruction gradually permeates to the four extremities. They converge upon the supreme standard and return to it, becoming inwardly transformed in a spirit of expansiveness [?]. The good order spoken of under Xia and Shang would again…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
見於今矣是則治內以先外則體統正而朝廷
之德澤流而天下化制治保邦孰有大于此哉
抑於是而知兆民之命繫於九牧而懸於六卿
六卿率屬而各得其人則政治無不明以倡九
牧而通行於天下矣是故舉於卿承於牧善則
兆民蒙其福舉於卿承於牧不善則兆民被其
殃舜命四岳九官十二牧而天下治良以親賢
爲急成王首立公孤而卽以此訓六卿可謂知
所重矣此其成重熙累洽之治也與吁周官六
典至今行之無弊所謂雖百世可知也
===
詩
蓼彼蕭斯零露湑兮既見君子我心寫兮
燕笑語兮是以有譽處兮
晉應槐

王者燕諸侯輿其情治而有以獲乎上焉甚矣
punctuated:
見於今矣。是則治內以先外，則體統正，而朝廷之德澤流，而天下化。制治保邦，孰有大于此哉？抑於是而知兆民之命繫於九牧而懸於六卿。六卿率屬而各得其人，則政治無不明，以倡九牧而通行於天下矣。是故舉於卿，承於牧，善則兆民蒙其福；舉於卿，承於牧，不善則兆民被其殃。舜命四岳、九官、十二牧而天下治，良以親賢爲急。成王首立公孤，而卽以此訓六卿，可謂知所重矣。此其成重熙累洽之治也與？吁！周官六典，至今行之無弊，所謂雖百世可知也。

王者燕諸侯，輿其情治而有以獲乎上焉。甚矣！
translation_en:
…will appear again today. Thus, when the ordering of the inner realm precedes that of the outer realm, the governing hierarchy is set right, the court’s beneficence flows abroad, and all under Heaven are transformed. What could be greater than this for establishing good government and preserving the state? From this we also understand that the lives of the myriad people depend upon the nine regional governors and hang upon the six ministers. If the six ministers lead their subordinates and each secures the right men, government will everywhere be enlightened, providing a lead for the nine regional governors and extending throughout the realm. Thus, when measures initiated by the ministers and carried out by the regional governors are good, the myriad people receive their blessings; when such measures are bad, the myriad people suffer their calamities. Shun appointed the Four Mountains, the nine officials, and the twelve regional governors, and all under Heaven was well governed, precisely because he made drawing close to worthy men his urgent concern. King Cheng first established the Three Dukes and Three Solitaries, and immediately used this teaching to instruct the six ministers. He may indeed be said to have understood what mattered most. Was this how he achieved a reign of accumulated brilliance and enduring harmony? Ah! The six statutes of the Offices of Zhou can still be put into practice today without ill effect. This is what is meant by saying that even a hundred generations hence may be known.

Book of Odes

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
人臣獲上之難也王者情洽於諸侯而樂是以
慰之斯其爲上下之交乎此諸侯來朝天子與
之燕以示慈惠也蓋曰朝覲之禮所以明君臣
燕饗之典所以仁賓客爾旣來朝以盡其禮則
所以待之之典何如哉彼蕭地產也露天澤也
惟蕭之本乎地也蓼然以長而妙夫上承之機
則露之零於天也湑然以繁而沛夫下被之澤
是露無心於蕭而蕭自有以致之蕭無心於露
而露自有以滋之此固物理感應之必然也而
===
況君子之在國也如弗克見每恨其相遇之疎
而其至止於斯也得侍同朝旣遂其就見之願
則所以隆其晉接之禮也惡容已乎是故與之
燕焉大烹以饗鐘鼓以樂禮意之厚蓋有出於
飲食之外者矣與之笑且語焉有言必吐有懷
必盡悅懌之情蓋有不拘於名分之嚴者矣夫
居下以獲上爲幸而人臣以得君爲難情意旣
洽於相通則名位可保於無斁是雖無心於要
譽也而羨其恩意之厚者令聞自爲之不已在
punctuated: 人臣獲上之難也！王者情洽於諸侯而樂，是以慰之，斯其爲上下之交乎？此諸侯來朝，天子與之燕以示慈惠也。蓋曰：朝覲之禮，所以明君臣；燕饗之典，所以仁賓客。爾旣來朝以盡其禮，則所以待之之典何如哉？彼蕭，地產也；露，天澤也。惟蕭之本乎地也，蓼然以長，而妙夫上承之機；則露之零於天也，湑然以繁，而沛夫下被之澤。是露無心於蕭，而蕭自有以致之；蕭無心於露，而露自有以滋之。此固物理感應之必然也。而況君子之在國也，如弗克見，每恨其相遇之疎；而其至止於斯也，得侍同朝，旣遂其就見之願，則所以隆其晉接之禮也，惡容已乎？是故與之燕焉，大烹以饗，鐘鼓以樂，禮意之厚，蓋有出於飲食之外者矣。與之笑且語焉，有言必吐，有懷必盡，悅懌之情，蓋有不拘於名分之嚴者矣。夫居下以獲上爲幸，而人臣以得君爲難。情意旣洽於相通，則名位可保於無斁。是雖無心於要譽也，而羨其恩意之厚者，令聞自爲之不已。在
translation_en: … how difficult it is for a subject to gain his sovereign’s favor! The king delights in the affection that unites him with the feudal lords and therefore comforts them. Is this not fellowship between sovereign and subjects? Here the feudal lords have come to court, and the Son of Heaven feasts with them to show his kindness and generosity. The meaning is this: the rites of court audience clarify the relationship between ruler and subject; the ceremonies of feasting treat guests with benevolence. Since you have come to court and fully discharged your ritual obligations, what ceremonies should be used to receive you? That southernwood is a product of the earth; the dew is heaven’s bounty. Rooted in the earth, the southernwood grows tall, wondrously receptive to what descends from above; falling from heaven, the dew gathers abundantly, lavishly bestowing its moisture below. The dew has no conscious intention toward the southernwood, yet the southernwood naturally draws it down; the southernwood has no conscious intention toward the dew, yet the dew naturally nourishes it. This is indeed the inevitable mutual responsiveness inherent in the principles of things. How much more so with these noble lords! While they remain in their own states, it seems impossible to see them, and one continually regrets how seldom meetings occur. When they arrive here and can attend the same court, the wish to meet is fulfilled. How, then, could one refrain from honoring them with the fullest ceremonies of reception? Thus he feasts with them, entertaining them with sumptuous dishes and delighting them with bells and drums. The generous spirit of these rites surely extends beyond food and drink. He laughs and converses with them: whatever there is to say is spoken, and whatever is felt is fully expressed. Their feelings of delight are surely unconstrained by the strict distinctions of rank. Those below count it fortunate to gain favor from above, while subjects find it difficult to win their ruler’s regard. Once their feelings are harmoniously joined through mutual communication, their standing and rank can be preserved without wearying of one another. Though they have no intention of seeking praise, those who admire the depth of their gracious affection naturally keep their good reputation alive. Among …

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
彼無惡在此無斁雖巧壬之言不足以間之其
諸茂來章之慶矣乎雖無心於固寵也而諒其
忠藎之忱者眷顧自為之有終長保其貴長守
其富雖怏懸之徒不足以危之其諸永保艾之
休矣乎夫如是則君信其臣而臣媚其君在臣
非干澤而在君非私惠也有周明良相慶之氣
象可想見矣雖然虞夏君臣交相儆戒周庭上
下多事燕樂所以然者豈其道固不相沿耶殊
不知都俞之中寓喜起之意諷誦之餘潛箴規
===
之志帝王異世而同道詩書異辭而同旨要不
可以二觀也故讀蓼蕭之詩者當逆作者之志
不然則會同之典適以為煩燕樂之儀祇以為
瀆君臣交慶之意微矣詩可以觀其此類也夫
濟濟多士文王以寧
于邦棟
同考試官教授萬　批〔周士傳世之顯正以有安民之功民安則文王安士子多說不出此作得之故錄〕
考試官教諭袁　批〔盛時氣象躍如〕
punctuated:
彼無惡，在此無斁，雖巧壬之言不足以間之，其諸茂來章之慶矣乎！雖無心於固寵也，而諒其忠藎之忱者，眷顧自為之有終。長保其貴，長守其富，雖怏懸之徒不足以危之，其諸永保艾之休矣乎！夫如是，則君信其臣，而臣媚其君；在臣非干澤，而在君非私惠也。有周明良相慶之氣象，可想見矣。雖然，虞夏君臣交相儆戒，周庭上下多事燕樂，所以然者，豈其道固不相沿耶？殊不知都俞之中寓喜起之意，諷誦之餘潛箴規之志。帝王異世而同道，詩書異辭而同旨，要不可以二觀也。故讀《蓼蕭》之詩者，當逆作者之志。不然，則會同之典適以為煩，燕樂之儀祇以為瀆，君臣交慶之意微矣。詩可以觀，其此類也夫！

濟濟多士，文王以寧。
于邦棟
同考試官教授萬　批〔周士傳世之顯，正以有安民之功。民安則文王安。士子多說不出，此作得之，故錄。〕
考試官教諭袁　批〔盛時氣象躍如。〕
translation_en:
…On the ruler’s side there is no aversion; on the minister’s side there is no weariness. Even the words of crafty flatterers cannot drive them apart. Surely this is the blessing of abundant, manifest favor! Although the minister has no intention of securing his hold on favor, the ruler, recognizing the sincerity of his devoted loyalty, naturally sustains his regard to the end. The minister long preserves his noble standing and his wealth; even resentful men [?] cannot endanger him. Surely this is the felicity of forever retaining favor! Thus the ruler trusts his minister, and the minister delights his ruler. The minister is not soliciting favors, nor is the ruler bestowing private benefits. We can picture the spirit of the Zhou age, when an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers rejoiced in one another.

Nevertheless, the rulers and ministers of Yu and Xia admonished one another, whereas superiors and subordinates at the Zhou court frequently engaged in feasting and music. Was this because their Way did not follow the same tradition? This overlooks how expressions of assent contained the spirit of joyful mutual encouragement, while recitation concealed the intent to admonish and correct. The sage sovereigns lived in different ages but followed the same Way; the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents differ in wording but share the same purport. They must not ultimately be regarded as two distinct teachings. Thus, readers of the ode “Luxuriant Southernwood” (Liao xiao) should seek to understand its author’s intention. Otherwise, the ceremonies of assembly become merely burdensome, and the rites of feasting and music merely disrespectful; the meaning of ruler and ministers rejoicing in one another is obscured. Is this not an example of how the Odes enable us to observe?

“Numerous were the accomplished officers; through them King Wen enjoyed peace.”

Yu Bangdong.

Associate Examiner Wan, Professor, comments: 〔The distinction of the Zhou officers through successive generations arose precisely from their achievement in bringing peace to the people. When the people were at peace, King Wen was at peace. Candidates generally fail to articulate this. This composition grasps it, and therefore it has been selected for inclusion.〕

Examiner Yuan, Instructor, comments: 〔The spirit of a flourishing age springs vividly to life.〕

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭顧　批〔雅健〕
詩人推周士有安上之功以見傳世之宜顯也
蓋人臣事上莫大乎能安之也而周之多士以
之其傳世之顯也宜哉此周公戒成王之詩也
至此若曰人臣立勛於國而後流慶於家周士
所以傳世之顯者是豈無其故乎彼士而匪賢
也固無以爲資理之寄賢而匪多也亦無以成
共理之功茲者庶明應運而興悉得於彙征之
吉楨榦爲周而樹允協乎勵翼之猷百僚師師
===
有疏附焉有先後焉每懷靡盬之憂無或有曠
厥官者矣吉人藹藹有奔奏焉有禦侮焉均矢
匪躬之節無或有爽厥志者矣夫多賢如此不
有以必文王之安乎吾知才賢之既昌固有以
符將興之兆而同道之相濟益有以崇致治之
休由是而濬明亮采莫不各以求莫之心爲心
謨明弼諧亦莫不同以敉寧之事爲事視民如
傷人見其文王之有憂矣不知疏附先後咸有
以先之穆穆文王不其恭已南面已乎不遑暇
punctuated:
考試官教諭顧　批〔雅健〕

詩人推周士有安上之功，以見傳世之宜顯也。蓋人臣事上，莫大乎能安之也，而周之多士以之，其傳世之顯也宜哉！此周公戒成王之詩也。至此，若曰：人臣立勛於國，而後流慶於家。周士所以傳世之顯者，是豈無其故乎？彼士而匪賢也，固無以爲資理之寄；賢而匪多也，亦無以成共理之功。茲者庶明應運而興，悉得於彙征之吉；楨榦爲周而樹，允協乎勵翼之猷。百僚師師，有疏附焉，有先後焉，每懷靡盬之憂，無或有曠厥官者矣。吉人藹藹，有奔奏焉，有禦侮焉，均矢匪躬之節，無或有爽厥志者矣。夫多賢如此，不有以必文王之安乎？吾知才賢之既昌，固有以符將興之兆，而同道之相濟，益有以崇致治之休。由是而濬明亮采，莫不各以求莫之心爲心；謨明弼諧，亦莫不同以敉寧之事爲事。視民如傷，人見其文王之有憂矣，不知疏附先後咸有以先之。穆穆文王，不其恭已南面已乎？不遑暇
translation_en:
Examiner Gu, Instructor, comments: 〔Elegant and vigorous.〕

The poet praises the service rendered by Zhou’s officers in bringing security to their sovereign, thereby showing why their distinction deserved to endure through successive generations. In serving his sovereign, a minister can achieve nothing greater than securing his peace; the many officers of Zhou accomplished this [?]. How fitting that their distinction should endure through the generations! This is a poem in which the Duke of Zhou admonishes King Cheng. At this point, it seems to say: Only after ministers establish merit in the state do blessings flow onward to their families. Could there be no reason why the officers of Zhou enjoyed such distinction through successive generations? If those officers were not worthy, they could certainly not be entrusted with assisting in government; if they were worthy but not numerous, neither could they accomplish the work of governing together.

Now men of understanding arose in response to the age, all enjoying the good fortune of advancing together. Pillars and beams were erected for Zhou, fully consonant with the purpose of diligent assistance. The hundred officials took one another as models: some brought the distant near and secured their allegiance; others guided and assisted. Each was ever mindful of his unremitting duties, and none neglected his office. Worthy men abounded: some hastened to carry out affairs; others resisted aggression. All alike pledged themselves to selfless integrity, and none departed from his resolve. With worthy men so numerous, was there not ample means to ensure King Wen’s peace?

I know that the flourishing of talented and worthy men fulfilled the auspicious signs of a coming rise; their mutual assistance in a shared Way further enhanced the excellence of good government. Thus, in exercising profound understanding and faithfully performing their duties, each made the pursuit of settled order [?] his own concern. In enlightened counsel and harmonious assistance, all likewise made the work of securing peace their common task. He regarded the people as though they were injured: people saw in this King Wen’s anxiety, but did not realize that those who drew others near, secured their allegiance, guided, and assisted all anticipated his needs. Did not solemn and dignified King Wen simply maintain a reverent bearing as he faced south upon the throne? With no leisure to …

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
食亦見其文王之爲勞矣不知奔奏禦侮悉有
以代之亹亹文王其亦垂衣聽治已乎信乎多
士不獨安一國之民而文王之心之身咸亦賴
以爲安矣輔世之功如此則其傳世之顯也亦
宜文德格天之慶於是乎不可忘矣噫豈文王
之倖致哉亹亹者心之所由以純也克生者賢
之所由以親也心純則有以爲招徠之本賢親
則有以動奮庸之機由是而起寅亮之忠享報
禮之重媢嫉一人者莫不計安社稷矣否則何
===
代無賢而惟周室爲得人之盛乎故曰純心要
矣用賢急焉繼文王者其知所監也夫厥后成
王嗣守大訓緝熙單心可謂善念爾祖者矣嗚
呼亦賢矣哉
春秋
夏宋人齊人衛人伐鄭〔莊公十有六年〕楚
屈完來盟于師〔僖公四年〕十有一月壬
戌晉侯及秦伯戰于韓獲晉侯〔僖公十
有五年〕
punctuated:
食，亦見其文王之爲勞矣。不知奔奏禦侮，悉有以代之，亹亹文王，其亦垂衣聽治已乎！信乎，多士不獨安一國之民，而文王之心之身，咸亦賴以爲安矣。輔世之功如此，則其傳世之顯也亦宜，文德格天之慶於是乎不可忘矣。噫！豈文王之倖致哉？亹亹者，心之所由以純也；克生者，賢之所由以親也。心純則有以爲招徠之本，賢親則有以動奮庸之機。由是而起寅亮之忠，享報禮之重，媢嫉一人者莫不計安社稷矣。否則，何代無賢，而惟周室爲得人之盛乎？故曰：純心要矣，用賢急焉。繼文王者，其知所監也夫！厥后成王嗣守大訓，緝熙單心，可謂善念爾祖者矣。嗚呼！亦賢矣哉！

春秋

夏，宋人、齊人、衛人伐鄭。〔莊公十有六年〕楚屈完來盟于師。〔僖公四年〕十有一月壬戌，晉侯及秦伯戰于韓，獲晉侯。〔僖公十有五年〕
translation_en:
…to eat: this, too, shows how King Wen toiled. Yet one does not realize that those who hurried about his business and resisted aggression could all take his place in these tasks. Diligent King Wen could thus let his robes hang down and attend to government without exertion! Truly, the many worthy men brought peace not only to the people of an entire state: King Wen himself, in both mind and body, also relied upon them for repose. Such were their achievements in assisting the age that their illustrious reputation in later generations was fitting. The blessing of civil virtue reaching Heaven must therefore never be forgotten.

Ah! Was this something King Wen attained by mere good fortune? His diligence was what made his heart pure; the successful birth of worthy men was what enabled him to draw them close. A pure heart provided the foundation for attracting them, and closeness to the worthy supplied the impetus for their vigorous service. Thus their loyal resolve to assist him reverently arose, and they enjoyed generous rewards and honors. Those who were jealous of the one man [?] all devised ways to secure the altars of soil and grain. Otherwise, what age has lacked worthy men? Why, then, was the house of Zhou alone so abundantly successful in obtaining their service? Hence it is said: purity of heart is essential, and employing the worthy is urgent. May those who succeed King Wen know where to find their model! Thereafter King Cheng inherited and upheld the great teachings, continuing to illuminate them and devoting his whole heart to them. He may indeed be said to have fulfilled well the injunction, “Be mindful of your ancestor.” Ah! How worthy he was!

Spring and Autumn Annals

In summer, men of Song, Qi, and Wei attacked Zheng. 〔The sixteenth year of Duke Zhuang.〕 Qu Wan of Chu came to conclude a covenant at the army’s camp. 〔The fourth year of Duke Xi.〕 In the eleventh month, on the renxu day, the Marquis of Jin fought the Earl of Qin at Han; the Marquis of Jin was captured. 〔The fifteenth year of Duke Xi.〕

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
瞿廷楠
同考試官教授宋　批〔敘事整潔斷案森嚴曲盡〕
書法之義
考試官教諭袁　批〔詞嚴而整〕
考試官教諭顧　批〔謹嚴〕
春秋紀霸國之節兵而因以無敵于天下也此
見桓仲所以成南權西抑之功者由其用節制
之兵也故春秋紀其實以善之焉吾聞内安外
攘匡天下之義也恤民薄賦息天下之仁也春
===
秋諸侯知此者鮮矣今也齊桓圖霸會北杏而
合諸侯管仲得君作内政以行軍令故自滅譚
之餘至今伐鄭之役討其背鄄之會而以將則
卑未嘗用大夫以將兵也正其侵宋之罪而以
師則少不必動大衆以即戎也是其以制用兵
既不盡人之力而因兵定賦亦不盡人之財矣
由是蓄養之威久而敵國自歸富强之業成而
外患自戢故南莫强于荆楚也而不戰有以摧
之寔征之命方申納款之誠恐後屈完定盟蓋
punctuated:
瞿廷楠

同考試官教授宋批〔敘事整潔，斷案森嚴，曲盡〕書法之義。
考試官教諭袁批〔詞嚴而整〕
考試官教諭顧批〔謹嚴〕

春秋紀霸國之節兵，而因以無敵于天下也。此見桓仲所以成南權西抑之功者，由其用節制之兵也。故春秋紀其實以善之焉。吾聞内安外攘，匡天下之義也；恤民薄賦，息天下之仁也。春秋諸侯知此者鮮矣。今也齊桓圖霸，會北杏而合諸侯；管仲得君，作内政以行軍令。故自滅譚之餘，至今伐鄭之役，討其背鄄之會，而以將則卑，未嘗用大夫以將兵也；正其侵宋之罪，而以師則少，不必動大衆以即戎也。是其以制用兵，既不盡人之力，而因兵定賦，亦不盡人之財矣。由是蓄養之威久而敵國自歸，富强之業成而外患自戢。故南莫强于荆楚也，而不戰有以摧之。寔征之命方申，納款之誠恐後。屈完定盟，蓋…
translation_en:
Qu Tingnan

Associate Examiner Song, Professor, comments: “The narration is orderly and clear, the judgments rigorously drawn, fully elucidating” the significance of the annalistic wording.
Examiner Yuan, Instructor, comments: “The language is rigorous and orderly.”
Examiner Gu, Instructor, comments: “Careful and rigorous.”

The Spring and Autumn Annals records how the hegemonic state exercised restraint in warfare and thereby became unrivaled under Heaven. This shows that Duke Huan and Guan Zhong achieved their influence in the south [?] and their restraint of the western powers through the use of disciplined, regulated forces. Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals records the facts to commend them. I have heard that securing order within and repelling threats without constitute the righteousness that sets the world aright; caring for the people and lightening taxation constitute the benevolence that brings the world repose. Few lords of the Spring and Autumn period understood this.

Now Duke Huan of Qi sought hegemony, convening the meeting at Beixing to unite the lords. Guan Zhong found a ruler who trusted him and organized domestic administration to implement military commands. Thus, from the aftermath of the destruction of Tan down to the present campaign against Zheng, when punishing Zheng for turning its back on the covenant at Juan, Qi employed commanders of low rank, never appointing grandees to lead its troops. When correcting Zheng’s offense of invading Song, it employed only a small force, without needing to mobilize a great host for war. By employing troops according to established regulations, it did not exhaust the people’s strength; by assessing levies according to military requirements, it likewise did not exhaust their wealth.

Consequently, as the power nurtured and sustained over time endured, rival states submitted of their own accord; as the work of building wealth and strength reached fruition, external troubles subsided of themselves. Thus, in the south, none was stronger than Jing-Chu, yet Qi had the means to break its resistance without battle. The command to undertake the punitive expedition had only just been proclaimed when Chu hastened to demonstrate its sincerity in submitting, fearful of being late. title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
先有以服其心也不然兩廣荆兵之衆方城漢
水之强求其不爲諸姬患也難矣而遽肯服於
齊哉西莫强於秦晉也而先聲有以抑之威加
于兩國而不爭兵息於二紀而不出韓原始戰
蓋先有以奪其氣也否則潼關百二之邦表裏
山河之盛欲其不爲中原擾也難矣而顧肯屈
於齊哉故春秋於伐鄭稱人紀其將卑師少之
實也又紀盟楚戰韓于後者著其以制用兵之
效也于此見桓公明足以知人而管仲才足以
===
佐霸君臣合而功烈著此春秋所以不可無桓
公而桓公不可無管仲乎雖然能摧强楚而九
國之梗即與能抑秦晉而五爭之禍繼作昔之
節兵以威天下者何在耶蓋以力服人者人不
敢不服故僞而易離以德服人者人不忍不服
故誠而可久桓仲四十餘年之所經營者無非
以力假仁之事也故屈完雖盟而楚人益横秦
晉暫服而齊霸遂衰使桓不屑於霸功而管仲
稍知王道豈遽至是也哉故曰秦之技擊不如
punctuated:
先有以服其心也。不然，兩廣荆兵之衆，方城漢水之强，求其不爲諸姬患也難矣，而遽肯服於齊哉？西莫强於秦晉也，而先聲有以抑之，威加于兩國而不爭，兵息於二紀而不出。韓原始戰，蓋先有以奪其氣也。否則，潼關百二之邦，表裏山河之盛，欲其不爲中原擾也難矣，而顧肯屈於齊哉？故《春秋》於伐鄭稱人，紀其將卑師少之實也；又紀盟楚、戰韓于後者，著其以制用兵之效也。于此見桓公明足以知人，而管仲才足以佐霸，君臣合而功烈著。此《春秋》所以不可無桓公，而桓公不可無管仲乎？

雖然，能摧强楚而九國之梗即與，能抑秦晉而五爭之禍繼作，昔之節兵以威天下者何在耶？蓋以力服人者，人不敢不服，故僞而易離；以德服人者，人不忍不服，故誠而可久。桓仲四十餘年之所經營者，無非以力假仁之事也。故屈完雖盟而楚人益横，秦晉暫服而齊霸遂衰。使桓不屑於霸功，而管仲稍知王道，豈遽至是也哉？故曰：「秦之技擊不如
translation_en:
…because their hearts had already been brought into submission. Otherwise, with Jing’s numerous troops in its two Guang chariot divisions, and the strength of Fangcheng and the Han River, it would have been difficult to keep Chu from threatening the states of the Ji lineage. How, then, could it so readily have submitted to Qi? In the west, none were stronger than Qin and Jin, yet the advance report of Qi’s might was enough to restrain them. Its authority bore upon both states, and they refrained from contention; their armies rested for twenty-four years without taking the field. Only at Hanyuan did they begin to fight: their fighting spirit had already been broken. Otherwise, given the strategic strength of the land at Tongguan, where two could hold off a hundred, and the imposing mountains and rivers protecting Jin within and without, it would have been difficult to keep them from disturbing the Central Plain. How could they have consented to bow to Qi?

Thus, in recording the attack on Zheng, the Spring and Autumn Annals uses the designation “men,” recording the fact that the commanders were of low rank and the forces few. Its subsequent records of the covenant with Chu and the battle at Han demonstrate the effectiveness of employing troops under disciplined regulation. Here we see that Duke Huan possessed sufficient discernment to recognize men of ability, while Guan Zhong possessed sufficient talent to assist a hegemon. Ruler and minister worked together, and their achievements became illustrious. Is this why the Spring and Autumn Annals could not dispense with Duke Huan, and Duke Huan could not dispense with Guan Zhong?

Nevertheless, although they could check mighty Chu, obstruction involving the nine states immediately arose [?]; although they could restrain Qin and Jin, the calamity of five contests followed [?]. Where, then, was that former ability to overawe the world through disciplined troops? When people are subdued by force, they dare not withhold submission; their submission is therefore feigned, and they readily break away. When people are won over by virtue, they cannot bear to withhold submission; their submission is therefore sincere and can endure. Everything Duke Huan and Guan Zhong worked to establish over more than forty years amounted to using force while borrowing the guise of benevolence. Thus, although Qu Wan entered into a covenant, the people of Chu grew increasingly overbearing; Qin and Jin submitted briefly, but Qi’s hegemony subsequently declined. Had Duke Huan disdained hegemonic achievements, and had Guan Zhong understood even a little of the Kingly Way, how could matters have come to this so soon? Hence the saying: “Qin’s skill in striking in combat does not equal …

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
桓文之節制桓文之節制不如湯武之仁義然
則春秋之取桓仲其亦不得已夫
仲孫蔑會晉欒黶宋華元衛甯殖曹人莒
人邾人滕人薛人圍宋彭城〔襄公元年〕
馬鑠
同考試官教授宋　批〔深合傳意辭嚴義正當是春秋〕
名筆
考試官教諭袁　批〔筆力老健〕
考試官教諭顧　批〔文有思致有精神〕
===
春秋紀列卿之討叛邑必追書以謹王度焉蓋
地有定制王度之不可易也觀春秋以彭城係
宋而其義見矣且彭城曷爲而圍也自魚石之
納方旋而虛朾之盟再講晉於是合八國以圍
之歸五大夫而置諸瓠丘焉信義舉矣然考是
邑也楚旣取之卽楚之彭城也宋弗得而保矣
魚石受之卽魚石之彭城也宋弗得而有矣春
秋仍係之宋者何蓋先王之公天下也而疆域
各有其等焉庶侯之藩王國也而封守各有其
punctuated:
桓文之節制，桓文之節制不如湯武之仁義。」然則《春秋》之取桓仲，其亦不得已夫！

仲孫蔑會晉欒黶、宋華元、衛甯殖、曹人、莒人、邾人、滕人、薛人，圍宋彭城。〔襄公元年〕
馬鑠
同考試官教授宋　批〔深合傳意，辭嚴義正，當是春秋〕名筆。
考試官教諭袁　批〔筆力老健。〕
考試官教諭顧　批〔文有思致，有精神。〕

《春秋》紀列卿之討叛邑，必追書以謹王度焉。蓋地有定制，王度之不可易也。觀《春秋》以彭城係宋，而其義見矣。且彭城曷爲而圍也？自魚石之納方旋，而虛朾之盟再講，晉於是合八國以圍之，歸五大夫而置諸瓠丘焉，信義舉矣。然考是邑也，楚旣取之，卽楚之彭城也，宋弗得而保矣；魚石受之，卽魚石之彭城也，宋弗得而有矣。《春秋》仍係之宋者何？蓋先王之公天下也，而疆域各有其等焉；庶侯之藩王國也，而封守各有其
translation_en:
… the disciplined forces of Dukes Huan and Wen; yet the disciplined forces of Dukes Huan and Wen were inferior to the benevolence and righteousness of Tang and Wu.” Thus, was not the Spring and Autumn Annals’ approval of Duke Huan and Guan Zhong likewise a concession made for want of a better alternative?

“Zhongsun Mie met with Luan Yan of Jin, Hua Yuan of Song, Ning Zhi of Wei, and men of Cao, Ju, Zhu, Teng, and Xue, and besieged Pengcheng of Song.” 〔First year of Duke Xiang.〕
Ma Shuo
Associate Examiner Song, Prefectural School Professor, comments: “Closely accords with the meaning of the commentary; its language is rigorous and its principles correct. Surely a masterful writer on the Spring and Autumn Annals.”
Examiner Yuan, County School Instructor, comments: “The writing is mature and vigorous.”
Examiner Gu, County School Instructor, comments: “The composition has thoughtful subtlety and vitality.”

When the Spring and Autumn Annals records the high ministers’ punitive expedition against a rebellious town, it necessarily traces back its affiliation in the record, thereby scrupulously upholding royal institutions. For territorial arrangements have established rules, and royal institutions cannot be altered. Observe how the Spring and Autumn Annals attaches Pengcheng to Song, and its meaning becomes apparent. Why, then, was Pengcheng besieged? Yu Shi had only just been reinstated when the covenant at Xuting was renewed. Jin thereupon assembled eight states to besiege the town, brought back the five grandees, and placed them at Huqiu. This was indeed a righteous undertaking.

Yet consider this town: once Chu had seized it, it was Chu’s Pengcheng, and Song could no longer retain it; once Yu Shi had received it, it was Yu Shi’s Pengcheng, and Song could no longer possess it. Why does the Spring and Autumn Annals still attach it to Song? Because the former kings administered all under Heaven impartially, territorial domains each had their prescribed rank; and as the various lords served as bulwarks of the royal realm, their enfeoffed territories and responsibilities for guarding them each had their …

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
□焉惟玆彭城楚可得而取耶魚石可得而有
耶自周錫之以爲五等之制所以崇德象賢者
此也楚惡得而奪之自宋受之以備三恪之封
所以承統作賓者此也魚石惡得而據之今也
登不恪以市恩楚共則取之而不知王章之不
可紊恃不庭以抗禮魚石則受之而不思大分
之不可踰雖曰戍以三百乘楚已擅其地矣然
稽之典籍之所存則彭城猶宋茅土之公也雖
曰居以五大夫魚石已專其土矣然考之史冊
===
之所載則彭城仍宋分封之舊也故春秋必追
書以係之宋若曰此宋之彭城也取于楚而楚
不能易也據于魚石而魚石不能亂也此義行
則楚之患息而夷不得以干夏大防樹矣魚石
之罪明而臣不敢以挾君大分昭矣嚴于一字
之書而萬世之法寓焉此春秋所以非聖人莫
能作乎雖然下陽虞虢塞邑也而不係之虞虎
牢鄭之巖邑也而不係之鄭又何以與彭城異
乎蓋係以國者見據險以怙亂者之罪明王度
punctuated: □焉。惟玆彭城，楚可得而取耶？魚石可得而有耶？自周錫之以爲五等之制，所以崇德象賢者此也，楚惡得而奪之？自宋受之以備三恪之封，所以承統作賓者此也，魚石惡得而據之？今也，登不恪以市恩，楚共則取之，而不知王章之不可紊；恃不庭以抗禮，魚石則受之，而不思大分之不可踰。雖曰戍以三百乘，楚已擅其地矣，然稽之典籍之所存，則彭城猶宋茅土之公也；雖曰居以五大夫，魚石已專其土矣，然考之史冊之所載，則彭城仍宋分封之舊也。故春秋必追書以係之宋，若曰：「此宋之彭城也，取于楚而楚不能易也，據于魚石而魚石不能亂也。」此義行，則楚之患息，而夷不得以干夏，大防樹矣；魚石之罪明，而臣不敢以挾君，大分昭矣。嚴于一字之書，而萬世之法寓焉，此春秋所以非聖人莫能作乎？雖然，下陽，虞虢塞邑也，而不係之虞；虎牢，鄭之巖邑也，而不係之鄭，又何以與彭城異乎？蓋係以國者，見據險以怙亂者之罪，明王度
translation_en:
…[one illegible character]. As for this Pengcheng, could Chu rightfully seize it? Could Yu Shi rightfully possess it? Zhou originally bestowed it under the system of five ranks of nobility: this was how virtue was honored and worthy predecessors were emulated. How could Chu usurp it? Song originally received it as one of the fiefs of the Three Honored Houses, thereby continuing a dynastic succession and serving as a guest of the reigning dynasty. How could Yu Shi occupy it?

Now, promoting the disloyal to purchase their gratitude [?], Duke Gong of Chu seized it, unaware that royal statutes must not be thrown into disorder. Relying on one who refused attendance at court to claim equal standing, Yu Shi accepted it, without considering that the fundamental distinctions of rank must not be transgressed. Although Chu had already appropriated the territory, reportedly garrisoning it with three hundred chariots, examination of the surviving canonical records shows that Pengcheng remained Song’s rightful grant of thatch and soil. Although Yu Shi had already monopolized the territory, reportedly settling five grandees there, examination of the historical records shows that Pengcheng remained part of Song’s original enfeoffment.

Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals necessarily traces back its rightful ownership in recording it as belonging to Song. It is as though it said: “This is Song’s Pengcheng. Though seized by Chu, Chu cannot alter that fact; though occupied by Yu Shi, Yu Shi cannot overturn it.” When this principle prevails, the threat from Chu subsides, and the barbarians cannot encroach upon the Chinese states: the great boundary is established. Yu Shi’s guilt becomes clear, and a minister dares not coerce his ruler: the fundamental distinction of rank is made manifest. Strictness in the writing of a single character embodies a rule for ten thousand generations. Is this why none but a sage could have composed the Spring and Autumn Annals?

Nevertheless, Xiayang was a fortified town guarding Yu and Guo, yet it is not identified as belonging to Yu; Hulao was a stronghold of Zheng, yet it is not identified as belonging to Zheng. Why are these treated differently from Pengcheng? Identifying a place with its state exposes the guilt of those who occupy strategic strongholds to persist in rebellion and makes clear the royal norms…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
也不係以國者見棄險以啓亂者之失明侯度
也王度明則可以保天下侯度明則可以保一
國春秋立義之精豈可以一端求乎後世如南
陽之取於齊維州之棄於外殆未講春秋之義
耶
禮記
舉者莫能勝也行者莫能致也
薛一鶚
同考試官學正黎　批〔題難發揮辭不費而意足矣録如〕
===
此篇
考試官教諭袁　批〔意味雋永〕
考試官教諭顧　批〔才筆俊逸〕
聖人兩言仁道之難盡示人之勉於仁也甚矣
仁之難成也任重而道遠非中心安仁者其孰
能之夫子歎其難有以哉想其意若謂立人之
道有所謂仁焉統四德而兼衆善自其全體而
言則擬之於器自其不息而言則擬之於道而
其理一也試言之凡舉之可勝者非器之重也
punctuated:
也。不係以國者，見棄險以啓亂者之失，明侯度也。王度明，則可以保天下；侯度明，則可以保一國。春秋立義之精，豈可以一端求乎？後世如南陽之取於齊、維州之棄於外，殆未講春秋之義耶？

禮記
舉者莫能勝也，行者莫能致也。
薛一鶚
同考試官學正黎　批〔題難發揮，辭不費而意足矣。録如〕此篇。
考試官教諭袁　批〔意味雋永。〕
考試官教諭顧　批〔才筆俊逸。〕

聖人兩言仁道之難盡，示人之勉於仁也。甚矣，仁之難成也！任重而道遠，非中心安仁者，其孰能之？夫子歎其難，有以哉！想其意若謂：立人之道，有所謂仁焉，統四德而兼衆善。自其全體而言，則擬之於器；自其不息而言，則擬之於道，而其理一也。試言之：凡舉之可勝者，非器之重也。
translation_en:
…Those places whose names are not linked to a state reveal the fault of those who abandon strategic strongholds and thereby invite disorder, making clear the standards governing the feudal lords. When the standards governing kings are clear, All-under-Heaven can be preserved; when the standards governing feudal lords are clear, a single state can be preserved. How could the subtlety with which the Spring and Autumn Annals establishes moral principles be understood from just one aspect? In later ages, cases such as the taking of Nanyang from Qi and the abandonment of Weizhou to outsiders suggest that the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals had perhaps not been studied!

Record of Rites
“Those who lift it cannot bear its weight; those who travel it cannot reach its end.”
Xue Yi’e
Associate Examiner Li, an Instructor, comments: “The topic is difficult to expound, yet the wording is economical and the meaning fully expressed. Recorded as this essay [?].”
Examiner Yuan, an Instructor, comments: “Its meaning leaves a rich and lasting savor.”
Examiner Gu, an Instructor, comments: “The writing displays outstanding talent and effortless grace.”

With two statements about the difficulty of fully realizing the Way of benevolence, the Sage shows people that they must strive to practice benevolence. How very difficult it is to perfect benevolence! The burden is heavy and the road long: who could accomplish it unless inwardly at ease in benevolence? The Master had good reason to sigh over its difficulty! We may imagine his meaning to be this: among the principles by which a person establishes himself, there is what is called benevolence, which unites the four virtues and embraces all goodness. Viewed in its entirety, it is likened to a vessel; viewed in its ceaseless operation, it is likened to a road. Yet its underlying principle is one. Let us explain: whatever one can lift and bear is no heavy vessel…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
惟仁之爲器則重而莫能勝焉蓋渾然完具旣
無方體之可擬粹然靜正又非形器所能囿是
故奉持雖力每限於分量之易盈舉其偏者未
能會乎其全也負荷雖勤恒歉於容受之未虛
得其麤者鮮能極乎其精也蓋一疵尚存卽爲
成德之累而厥施或匱不免體物之遺則凡隨
所舉之多寡而以仁名者皆不得與矣果孰能
勝之乎凡行之可致者非道之遠也惟仁之爲
道則遠而莫能致焉蓋與生俱生妙其機於莫
===
禦與形俱形昭其運於不息是故健以致其決
也則幾非在我力或竭於半途原始要終者誰
與果以邁其行也則化不可爲功或虧於一簣
過此以往者誰與蓋一息尚存此志不容少懈
而終身由之道妙猶有未窺則凡隨所至之遠
近而以仁淥者皆不得有焉果孰能致之乎吁
仁道至大而難能如此君子當克愼其難以求
進於仁矣詎可自委於其重且遠耶抑夫子他
日又曰仁遠乎哉我欲仁斯仁至矣夫仁一也
punctuated: 惟仁之爲器，則重而莫能勝焉。蓋渾然完具，旣無方體之可擬；粹然靜正，又非形器所能囿。是故奉持雖力，每限於分量之易盈，舉其偏者未能會乎其全也；負荷雖勤，恒歉於容受之未虛，得其麤者鮮能極乎其精也。蓋一疵尚存，卽爲成德之累；而厥施或匱，不免體物之遺。則凡隨所舉之多寡而以仁名者，皆不得與矣。果孰能勝之乎？凡行之可致者，非道之遠也；惟仁之爲道，則遠而莫能致焉。蓋與生俱生，妙其機於莫禦；與形俱形，昭其運於不息。是故健以致其決也，則幾非在我，力或竭於半途，原始要終者誰與？果以邁其行也，則化不可爲，功或虧於一簣，過此以往者誰與？蓋一息尚存，此志不容少懈；而終身由之，道妙猶有未窺。則凡隨所至之遠近而以仁淥者，皆不得有焉。果孰能致之乎？吁！仁道至大而難能如此，君子當克愼其難，以求進於仁矣，詎可自委於其重且遠耶？抑夫子他日又曰：「仁遠乎哉？我欲仁，斯仁至矣。」夫仁一也，
translation_en:
…Only benevolence, considered as a vessel, is so heavy that none can bear it. Whole and complete, it has no fixed shape or form to which it can be likened; pure, still, and upright, it cannot be confined within material objects. Thus, however vigorously one upholds it, one is continually constrained by a capacity that too readily fills: those who take up one aspect cannot comprehend its entirety. However diligently one bears it, one remains deficient because one’s receptivity is not yet empty: those who grasp its coarse aspects seldom exhaust its subtleties. So long as a single flaw remains, it encumbers the perfection of virtue; and if its exercise is in any respect deficient, something is inevitably left out of its embodiment in things. Thus, those who give the name of benevolence to whatever greater or lesser portion they have taken up cannot be counted among those who possess it. Who, indeed, can bear it?

Whatever can be reached by walking does not exemplify the distance of this Way. Only benevolence, considered as a Way, is so distant that none can reach it. Arising together with life, its subtle workings cannot be checked; taking form together with bodily form, its operation is manifest in ceaseless activity. Thus, even when one vigorously brings one’s resolve to bear, the incipient workings are not within one’s control, and one’s strength may fail halfway. Who can trace the beginning and carry through to the end? Even when one advances resolutely in practice, transformation cannot be contrived, and the undertaking may fail for want of a single basketful of earth. Who can go onward beyond this? So long as a single breath remains, this aspiration must not slacken in the least; yet even after following it throughout one’s life, there are subtleties of the Way one has still not glimpsed. Thus, those who describe whatever nearer or farther point they have reached as benevolence [?] cannot possess it. Who, indeed, can reach it?

Ah! Since the Way of benevolence is so great and so difficult to realize, the gentleman should attend carefully to its difficulty and seek to advance in benevolence. How could he simply give up because of its weight and distance? Yet on another occasion the Master also said: “Is benevolence far away? If I desire benevolence, benevolence is here.” Now benevolence is one and the same…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
何此擬其難而復言其易與蓋仁道雖大而爲
仁由已故弘毅以立本則重遠可有矣克復以
爲學則天下歸仁矣仁果終不可體耶夫子此
言恐學者狃於其易而莫肯用力所以激而進
之也故曰聖人之言莫非至教
夫昔者君子比德於玉焉溫潤而澤仁也
縝密以栗知也廉而不劌義也垂之如
隊禮也叩之其聲淸越以長其終詘然
樂也瑕不揜瑜瑜不揜瑕忠也孚尹旁
===
達信也氣如白虹天也精神見于山川
地也圭璋特達德也天下莫不貴者道
也詩云言念君子溫其如玉故君子貴
之也
喬承詔
同考試官學正黎　批　〔題長作者不贅則泛是篇簡約〕
〔明備文之佳者〕
考試官教諭袁　批　沖腴
考試官教諭顧　批　縝密
punctuated:
何此擬其難，而復言其易與？蓋仁道雖大，而爲仁由已，故弘毅以立本，則重遠可有矣；克復以爲學，則天下歸仁矣。仁果終不可體耶？夫子此言，恐學者狃於其易而莫肯用力，所以激而進之也。故曰：聖人之言，莫非至教。

夫昔者君子比德於玉焉：溫潤而澤，仁也；縝密以栗，知也；廉而不劌，義也；垂之如隊，禮也；叩之，其聲淸越以長，其終詘然，樂也；瑕不揜瑜，瑜不揜瑕，忠也；孚尹旁達，信也；氣如白虹，天也；精神見于山川，地也；圭璋特達，德也；天下莫不貴者，道也。《詩》云：「言念君子，溫其如玉。」故君子貴之也。

喬承詔

同考試官學正黎，批：〔題長，作者不贅則泛，是篇簡約〕〔明備，文之佳者。〕

考試官教諭袁，批：沖腴。

考試官教諭顧，批：縝密。
translation_en:
…Why does he here portray its difficulty, yet elsewhere speak of its ease? Although the Way of benevolence is great, practicing benevolence depends on oneself. Thus, by establishing a foundation through breadth of spirit and firmness of resolve, one can manage the heavy burden and distant journey [?]; by making self-mastery and a return to ritual propriety the substance of learning, one brings all under Heaven back to benevolence. Can benevolence truly be impossible ever to embody? In saying this, the Master feared that learners would grow complacent about its ease and refuse to exert themselves; he therefore sought to rouse them and advance their progress. Thus it is said: none of the sage’s words fails to provide the highest instruction.

“In former times, the gentleman likened virtue to jade. Its warmth, smoothness, and luster signify benevolence; its fine, close texture and firmness, wisdom; its sharp edges that do not cut, righteousness; its hanging downward as though falling, ritual propriety. When struck, its sound is clear, carries far, and lingers, then comes to a distinct close: this signifies music. Its flaws do not conceal its beauty, nor does its beauty conceal its flaws: this signifies loyalty. Its radiance shines forth on every side: trustworthiness. Its vital emanation resembles a white rainbow: Heaven. Its spiritual essence manifests itself in mountains and rivers: Earth. The gui and zhang jade tablets are presented in their own right: virtue. That none under Heaven fails to esteem it signifies the Way. The Book of Odes says: ‘I think of that gentleman, warm and gentle as jade.’ Thus the gentleman esteems it.”

Qiao Chengzhao 喬承詔

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
聖人詳君子貴玉之由必引言以明之也夫玉
之爲貴也尚矣自非詳著其可貴之德人亦孰
從而知之哉昔夫子答子貢貴玉賤碈之問至
此若謂玉之貴于天下固非爲玉之寡矣而其
所可貴者何居蓋君子之于玉惟其以有心之
感而契乎無心之質故每以形下之器而方乎
形上之德獨不觀玉之德乎夫德之全體析而
分之有四端衆善之殊也而在玉則溫潤滑澤
爲仁之愛縝密堅栗爲知之貞廉隅不劌爲義
===
之斷垂之如隊爲禮之謙清越終詘爲樂之節
以至瑕瑜不掩爲忠之發孚尹旁達爲信之實
而德之殊者備矣統而會之有天地道德之大
也而在玉則氣如白虹而發天之光精神見于
山川而合地之靈以至圭璋特達具獨秉之懿
天下同貴若其由之理而德之大者備矣由在
玉各備乎德之美所以君子比德于玉之良詩
曰言念君子溫其如玉蓋謂是也是故君子不
以器視玉而崇尚之有加用之宗廟朝廷焉以
punctuated: 聖人詳君子貴玉之由，必引言以明之也。夫玉之爲貴也尚矣，自非詳著其可貴之德，人亦孰從而知之哉？昔夫子答子貢貴玉賤碈之問，至此若謂：玉之貴于天下，固非爲玉之寡矣，而其所可貴者何居？蓋君子之于玉，惟其以有心之感而契乎無心之質，故每以形下之器而方乎形上之德。獨不觀玉之德乎？夫德之全體，析而分之，有四端衆善之殊也。而在玉，則溫潤滑澤爲仁之愛，縝密堅栗爲知之貞，廉隅不劌爲義之斷，垂之如隊爲禮之謙，清越終詘爲樂之節，以至瑕瑜不掩爲忠之發，孚尹旁達爲信之實，而德之殊者備矣。統而會之，有天地道德之大也。而在玉，則氣如白虹而發天之光，精神見于山川而合地之靈，以至圭璋特達，具獨秉之懿，天下同貴，若其由之理，而德之大者備矣。由在玉各備乎德之美，所以君子比德于玉之良。詩曰：「言念君子，溫其如玉。」蓋謂是也。是故君子不以器視玉，而崇尚之有加，用之宗廟朝廷焉，以
translation_en:
In explaining fully why the gentleman esteems jade, the sage necessarily cites a saying to make the matter clear. Jade has been esteemed since remote antiquity. Unless its estimable virtues were set forth in detail, how could people come to understand them? Formerly, when the Master answered Zigong’s question about esteeming jade and slighting the stone called min, at this point he seemed to be saying: Jade is esteemed throughout the world certainly not because it is scarce. What, then, makes it worthy of esteem? In his relation to jade, the gentleman’s conscious responsiveness accords with its insentient substance. Thus he regularly compares a tangible object with virtues that transcend tangible form. Have you not considered jade’s virtues?

When virtue in its entirety is analyzed into its constituent parts, there are the distinctions among the four beginnings and the manifold forms of goodness. In jade, its warmth, moistness, smoothness, and sheen embody the love of benevolence; its fine texture, solidity, and firmness embody the steadfastness of wisdom; its angular edges, which do not cut, embody the decisiveness of righteousness; its hanging down as though falling embodies the humility of ritual propriety; and its clear, far-reaching tone, which finally dies away, embodies the measured order of music. Moreover, its flaws and beauty, neither concealing the other, embody the expression of loyalty, while its lustre, radiating in every direction, embodies the substance of trustworthiness. Thus the distinct aspects of virtue are all present.

Taken together as a unified whole, there is the greatness of Heaven, Earth, the Way, and virtue. In jade, its vital emanation resembles a white rainbow and manifests Heaven’s radiance; its spiritual essence appears in mountains and rivers and accords with Earth’s numinous power. Furthermore, the gui and zhang jade tablets, presented on their own, possess an excellence uniquely their own; jade is esteemed by all under Heaven, resembling the principle they follow [?]. Thus the great dimensions of virtue are all present. Since jade possesses each of these beauties of virtue [?], the gentleman compares virtue to the excellence of jade. The Book of Odes says: “When I think of the gentleman, he is as warm and gentle as jade.” This is surely what it means.

Therefore, the gentleman does not regard jade merely as an object, but esteems it all the more, employing it in the ancestral temple and at court in order to…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
重其精粹之蘊也不以貨視玉而尊異之惟謹
用之祭聘服具焉爲寶其純一之質也君子之
貴玉也如此則其有如玉之德不由是而可知
也耶孔子具溫良恭儉讓之容上律下襲道全
德備身有玉之德矣所以論玉之可貴眞切詳
悉如此也奈何聖人之時貴玉者多而知德者
鮮使孔子有美玉於斯韞匵藏諸之歎而玉終
莫之售也雖然圭璧瑚璉輝映後世其視崇用
於當時者顧孰多乎噫
===
第貳場
論
學以至乎聖人之道　　　　薛一鶚
同考試官學正黎　批〔議論雄渾筆力高古迥異塵作〕
宜錄以式多士
考試官教諭袁　批〔闔闢操縱法度森嚴〕
考試官教諭顧　批〔氣昌理到知潛心之學者〕
聖人純乎天而極學聖人者亦純乎聖人之天
punctuated:
重其精粹之蘊也。不以貨視玉，而尊異之惟謹，用之祭聘服具焉，爲寶其純一之質也。君子之貴玉也如此，則其有如玉之德，不由是而可知也耶？孔子具溫良恭儉讓之容，上律下襲，道全德備，身有玉之德矣。所以論玉之可貴，眞切詳悉如此也。奈何聖人之時，貴玉者多，而知德者鮮，使孔子有「美玉於斯，韞匵藏諸」之歎，而玉終莫之售也。雖然，圭璧瑚璉，輝映後世，其視崇用於當時者，顧孰多乎？噫！

第貳場
論
學以至乎聖人之道　薛一鶚

同考試官學正黎批〔議論雄渾，筆力高古，迥異塵作〕宜錄以式多士。
考試官教諭袁批〔闔闢操縱，法度森嚴〕
考試官教諭顧批〔氣昌理到，知潛心之學者〕

聖人純乎天而極，學聖人者亦純乎聖人之天
translation_en:
…to honor the refined essence contained within it. They do not regard jade as merchandise, but take the utmost care to accord it special esteem. They use it in sacrifices, diplomatic exchanges, and articles of attire because they treasure its pure and undivided substance. Since gentlemen esteem jade in this way, can we not thereby recognize that they possess virtues like those of jade? Confucius displayed warmth, goodness, respectfulness, frugality, and deference. Above, he followed Heaven’s patterns; below, he conformed to Earth. His Way was complete and his virtue fully realized: he himself possessed the virtues of jade. Thus his discussion of jade’s preciousness was so true, pertinent, detailed, and comprehensive. Yet how was it that, in the sage’s time, many esteemed jade but few understood virtue, prompting Confucius to lament, “Here is a beautiful jade: should I store it away in a casket?” In the end, the jade found no buyer. Nevertheless, these jade tablets and disks, these precious sacrificial vessels, shine upon later generations. Compared with being honored and employed in his own time, which has the greater worth? Ah!

Second Session
Discourse
“Through Learning, Attain the Way of the Sage” — Xue Yi’e

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
而極夫天者理也理者心也聖人之純乎天惟
純乎理而已矣聖人之純乎理惟純乎心而已
矣心純則理純理純則天純合天人而一之聖
人於是乎不可及矣然聖人非有異於人也其
心同其理同聖人不過能盡其心以達諸天此
所以爲善事其天也衆人有天而不知事放心
越理而不之求卒使天人判聖狂分而道與我
始相遠矣苟能先明諸心務窮其理知聖人之
心本一也而吾亦不敢雜之知聖人之心本誠
===
也而吾亦不敢僞之審其幾於理欲之辨致其
力於克復之專由勉而求至於安由有迹以至
於無迹則聖人之天在我我其聖人矣又何天
何人何聖何我之有異耶程子論顏淵之好學
而曰學以至乎聖人之道蓋以心明聖人而欲
人知所學也且人之生也性本貞靜所謂繼之
者善成之者性也及其有感而動而情始出焉
所謂有物有則秉彝好德者也斯二者皆天也
天豈有擇於人而爲之增損者哉惟聖人盡性
punctuated:
而極。夫天者，理也；理者，心也。聖人之純乎天，惟純乎理而已矣；聖人之純乎理，惟純乎心而已矣。心純則理純，理純則天純，合天人而一之，聖人於是乎不可及矣。然聖人非有異於人也，其心同，其理同，聖人不過能盡其心以達諸天，此所以爲善事其天也。衆人有天而不知事，放心越理而不之求，卒使天人判、聖狂分，而道與我始相遠矣。苟能先明諸心，務窮其理，知聖人之心本一也，而吾亦不敢雜之；知聖人之心本誠也，而吾亦不敢僞之。審其幾於理欲之辨，致其力於克復之專，由勉而求至於安，由有迹以至於無迹，則聖人之天在我，我其聖人矣。又何天、何人、何聖、何我之有異耶？程子論顏淵之好學，而曰：「學以至乎聖人之道。」蓋以心明聖人，而欲人知所學也。

且人之生也，性本貞靜，所謂「繼之者善，成之者性」也。及其有感而動，而情始出焉，所謂「有物有則，秉彝好德」者也。斯二者皆天也。天豈有擇於人而爲之增損者哉？惟聖人盡性
translation_en:
…and attain the utmost. Heaven is principle; principle is the heart-mind. The sage’s purity in accord with Heaven is simply purity in accord with principle; his purity in accord with principle is simply purity of the heart-mind. When the heart-mind is pure, principle is pure; when principle is pure, Heaven is pure. By joining Heaven and humanity into one, the sage becomes unattainable to others. Yet the sage is not different from other people: his heart-mind is the same, and his principle is the same. The sage is simply able to realize his heart-mind fully and thereby reach Heaven. This is what makes him adept at serving the Heaven within him. Ordinary people possess Heaven but do not know how to serve it. They let their heart-minds stray and transgress principle without seeking to recover them. Ultimately, Heaven and humanity become divided, and the sage and the fool part ways; only then does the Way become distant from us. If we can first attain clarity within the heart-mind and strive to fathom its principle, recognizing that the sage’s heart-mind is fundamentally undivided, we too will not dare introduce admixture into our own; recognizing that the sage’s heart-mind is fundamentally sincere, we too will not dare make our own false. We must scrutinize the incipient stirrings in distinguishing principle from desire, and devote our strength single-mindedly to overcoming the self and returning to ritual propriety. Advancing from effort toward ease, and from action that leaves traces to action without traces, we will then possess within ourselves the Heaven of the sage, and become sages ourselves. What distinction could then remain between Heaven and humanity, or between the sage and ourselves? Master Cheng, discussing Yan Yuan’s love of learning, said: “Through learning, attain the Way of the sage.” He explained sagehood through the heart-mind, wishing people to know what they should learn.

Moreover, when people are born, their nature is fundamentally upright and still. This is what is meant by: “What continues it is goodness; what brings it to completion is nature.” When they are moved in response to things, the emotions first emerge. This is what is meant by: “Where there are things, there are their norms; holding fast to their constant nature, people love virtue.” Both of these are Heaven. Could Heaven possibly discriminate among people, adding to some and taking away from others? Only the sage fully realizes his nature…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
以至於命天無不全而理無不得是故靜與天
俱動與天游而能自立於無過之地故以喜則
不濫以怒則不留以哀則不傷以樂則不淫發
皆中節施無不當則又何害於情何傷於性何
賊於心何拂於天始則天之未始不爲人終則
人亦未始不爲天矣但人之爲道不知以心爲
事而自遠其則行之而不著習矣而不察者衆
矣生而靜者奪於耳目之官平旦所息者梏於
晝之反覆蕩情亂性縱心悖天而始與聖人異
===
是豈人之性情哉故知性之本無惡也則知自
暴自棄之心不可有也知情之可以爲善也則
知存心養性之功不可緩也春秋之時求其知
此道者莫如孔子體此道者亦莫如孔子觀其
言曰性相近也習相遠也又曰君子上達小人
下達蓋傷天下之鑿其性也曰中心安仁天下
一人曰從心所欲不踰矩蓋勵天下之順其情
也當是時善學孔子者又孰有愈於顏子者乎
三月不違是雖未至於孔子也而其從事之勇
punctuated: 以至於命，天無不全，而理無不得。是故靜與天俱，動與天游，而能自立於無過之地。故以喜則不濫，以怒則不留，以哀則不傷，以樂則不淫，發皆中節，施無不當，則又何害於情，何傷於性，何賊於心，何拂於天？始則天之未始不爲人，終則人亦未始不爲天矣。但人之爲道，不知以心爲事，而自遠其則，行之而不著，習矣而不察者衆矣。生而靜者奪於耳目之官，平旦所息者梏於晝之反覆，蕩情亂性，縱心悖天，而始與聖人異。是豈人之性情哉？故知性之本無惡也，則知自暴自棄之心不可有也；知情之可以爲善也，則知存心養性之功不可緩也。春秋之時，求其知此道者，莫如孔子；體此道者，亦莫如孔子。觀其言曰：「性相近也，習相遠也。」又曰：「君子上達，小人下達。」蓋傷天下之鑿其性也。曰：「中心安仁，天下一人。」曰：「從心所欲，不踰矩。」蓋勵天下之順其情也。當是時，善學孔子者，又孰有愈於顏子者乎？三月不違，是雖未至於孔子也，而其從事之勇
translation_en: …and thereby reaches Heaven’s mandate: Heaven is wholly preserved, and principle fully apprehended. Thus, in stillness the sage abides with Heaven, and in movement roams with Heaven, establishing himself where he is free of error. His joy is not excessive, his anger does not linger, his sorrow does not wound, and his delight does not become unrestrained. His feelings, when expressed, all attain due measure, and their application is always fitting. How, then, could they harm his feelings, injure his nature, undermine his heart, or run counter to Heaven? At the outset, Heaven has never been apart from the human; in the end, the human, too, has never been apart from Heaven. Yet people, in pursuing the Way, do not know to make the heart their concern and thus distance themselves from their own standard. Many follow it without understanding it and become accustomed to it without examining it. The stillness with which they are born is overpowered by the faculties of hearing and sight; what has been replenished by dawn is fettered by the repeated disturbances of the day. They let their feelings run wild and disorder their nature, indulge their hearts and defy Heaven; only then do they become different from the sage. Can this truly be human nature and feeling? Thus, to know that human nature is originally without evil is to know that one must not harbor a heart that injures and abandons itself. To know that feelings can become good is to know that the work of preserving the heart and nourishing one’s nature must not be delayed. In the Spring and Autumn period, none understood this Way as well as Kongzi, and none embodied it as well as he did. Consider his words: “By nature, people are close to one another; through practice, they grow far apart.” He also said: “The gentleman advances toward what is higher; the petty man advances toward what is lower.” These words lament how people throughout the world mutilate their nature. It is said: “At ease in benevolence within his heart—he alone in all the world.” And he said: “I followed my heart’s desires without overstepping the bounds.” These words encourage people throughout the world to follow their feelings aright. At that time, who surpassed Yanzi in learning well from Kongzi? For three months he did not depart from benevolence. Although in this he had not yet attained Kongzi’s level, the courage with which he devoted himself to the task…

title: 嘉靖三十四年山西鄉試錄
text:
語之不惰眞有欲罷不能者視諸自畫願息不
亦大相十百者耶世之論顏者莫不曰步亦步
趨亦趨可以見其以實求孔子焉又莫不曰墮
體黜聰心齋坐忘可以見其以虛求孔子焉不
知虛實有無之間動靜形感之際顏子殆難以
形迹者拘矣自今觀之非禮勿視非禮勿聽非
禮勿言非禮勿動非以中禮者聖人而四勿復
禮者爲求聖之功乎不遷怒不貳過非以無過
無怒者聖人而不遷不貳者爲求聖之功乎明
===
以察幾犍以致決由不遷怒以求至於無怒由
不貳過以求至於無過由復禮以求至於中禮
約其情以合於中盡其性以契乎天顏子之心
蓋得孔子之意而忘言者多矣其動靜語默用
行舍藏何莫不與孔子似耶是故庶乎屢空一
孔子之浮雲富貴也願無伐善無施勞一孔子
之何有未能也終日如愚一孔子之無言默識
也有若無實若虛得一善拳拳服膺弗失一孔
子之爲學不厭也顏之去孔特未達一間耳曰
